maintopic: CANADA MEDICAL ACT-AMENDMENT.

speechtext: Mr. BLACK moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 15) to amend the Canada Medical Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CANADA MEDICAL ACT-AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Explain please.

maintopic: CANADA MEDICAL ACT-AMENDMENT.
speechtext: This is an Act to amend the present Canada Medical Act, sometimes known as the Ruddick Act. The pro-visons of the Bill are not many, nor are they important, except one which is intended to provide that any medical practitioner entitled to practise medicine in any province in Canada may be entitled to practise medicine all over Canada. This is the main feature of the Bill.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE-AUDITOR GENERAL.
PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE-AUDITOR GENERAL.
speechtext:
I would ask the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to have the Public Accounts Committee called for its first meeting at the earliest possible moment. I would suggest to-morrow morning. There will be a good deal of
work before that committee, and the sooner it begins that work the sooner the session will conclude. I believe that sometimes the organization of this committee has been delayed for a couple of weeks, or even three weeks, which has been found very inconvenient. It seems to me that not a minute should be lost, but that we should endeavour to get through the business of the House and committees as speedily as possible.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE-AUDITOR GENERAL.
speechtext: I have no objection to the suggestion although perhaps, to-morrow morning will be found too early a date. I will ask the Chief Whip of the government side to have the meeting called as early as possible-if not to-morrow, then the day after.

maintopic: TRANSPORTATION OF ANIMALS- ALLEGED DISREGARD OF RULES.
TRANSPORTATION OF ANIMALS- ALLEGED DISREGARD OF RULES.
speechtext:
I desire to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) to a statement which has been made to me, that the regulations for the transportation of animals between Canada and the United States are being disregarded, especially on the Wabash railway. Rule 3 provides:
All empty cars, whether of Canadian origin or not, entering Canada from the United States must, if not already showing evidence of having been so treated, be thoroughly cleansed and disinfected to the satisfaction of the inspectors of this department, otherwise they will be returned to the United States.
And section 6 provides:

After May 31,	1905, all cars conveying
swine from the United States into Canada, whether intended for transit to some other part of the United States or to points in Canada, must be fitted with ten-inch foot boards in a manner satisfactory to inspectors of this department.
It is very important that these rules should be strictly lived up to. In the county of Essex, which is one of the chief hog-producing counties of Canada, hog cholera broke out recently along the line of one of these railways. This is a very serious matter to farmers of that county, and no doubt, the minister will give it his attention.

maintopic: TRANSPORTATION OF ANIMALS- ALLEGED DISREGARD OF RULES.
speechtext: No complaint has reached me on this subject, nor has any reached the department so far as I know. But I will certainly draw the attention of the officers in charge to what has just been stated. I quite agree with the hon. member (Mr. Wilcox) that these rules should be strictly and efficiently enforced.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.

speechtext: House resumed adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. McGiverin : for an Address to His Excellency the Governor General, in reply to his speech at the opening of the session ; the proposed amendment of Mr. Monk thereto, and Mr. Borden's proposed amendment to the amendment.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the remarks I made before the adjournment of this debate on Friday night, I referred to the speech of the mover of the address (Mr. McGiverin) and spoke of the character of the debate up to that time and endeavoured to draw a few lessons from the tour of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in the west. The mover of the address dwelt on the great events, advances in the trade and commerce of the country during the past year using these words:
Reports from every section of the country show that it is only the ordinary general growth of the nation's trade, commerce and industry which is responsible for this wonderful showing.
These are wise words; and I think that when we are not playing to the gallery, we can all readily acquiesce in the statement that the intelligence and energy of the Canadian people, and the wealth of Canada's natural resources are the real cause of the prosperity of the country, and we should be less hypocritical if we acknowledged this frankly instead of trying to strengthen the government of the day by ascribing to it prosperity with which governments often have little to do. That government, after all, is the best which places Mr. WILCOX.
the fewest restrictions possible on its people, and which gives assistance, generous assistance, when that assistance is clearly in the interest of the whole state, and where honesty, coupled with efficiency, is the keynote of its administration of public affairs, and whose appointments to public office are [DOT]based solely on the merits of the appointees and are not of the nature of rewards for party services. We on this side claim that it is the lamentable failure of this government to reach these ideals that makes the strongest count against the present ministry. And, strong as is the indictment against the government on account of its naval policy, not less strong is the case against the government for the mal-admin-istration of public affairs, and its long and persistent refusal to investigate the great departments of state, and its equally persistent refusal to consult the people on matters of great national import-for, after all, they are the servants and not the masters of the people. It is this last indictment which is the subject matter of the amendments which are now before the House, and I propose to deal with them both in a general way, and also in relation to the question of the navy which has formed the special feature of "this debate. Government speakers have put before the House, and have endeavoured to establish before the country a number of propositions. The first which I have noted-and I have followed the various speakers pretty carefully-is the statement that the Conservative party is in alliance with the Nationalists, and has instigated or connived at unpatriotic, unworthy methods in the recent by-election in the province of Quebec. Around this the battle in this debate has raged. The most desperate arguments have been used by hon. gentlemen opposite to explain the shattering of the prestige of my right hon. friend in the province of Quebec. Assertions have been made, and methods adopted' in this House, even by a minister .of the Crown, that were absolutely unworthy of parliament; and my hon. friend from Argenteuil (Mr. Perley), who has the unqualified respect of every member of this House, had to rise in his seat the other day and repel an insinuation made by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) which should never have been made on the floor of this House. That insinuation was not the only thing which disfigured the speech of the hon. minister-in fact there were few redeeming traits in it. One of the pitiable features of the debate was the exhibition given by my hon. friend the member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) on Thursday night. My hon. friend was apparently put up to defend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and explain away the regrettable incident of the cartoon displayed by him.

But the more the hon. member from South Grey explained, the more apparent became the predicament into which the minister had fallen, and the worse his conduct appeared, so that he might well have exclaimed :	' Save me from my friends.'
I am sorry the hon. gentleman is not in his seat, but his explanation reminded me of a story about a man who shot his neighbour's dog, and I think it so applicable that I cannot refrain from giving it. A certain man shot his neighbour's dog by mistake and the neighbour, who was very furious, demanded an explanation. The offender attempted an apology and an explanation at very great length. In explaining the accident he got very excited, and in showing how, as he was shooting at a bird, the dog came between and got the charge, he pulled the trigger and shot his neighbour. In due course the coroner and his jury sat upon the corpse and called on the accused to explain his conduct. The accused, in the course of his explanation, again became very excited, and in showing how the accident occurred he again unconsciously drew the trigger and this time shot the coroner. Without any more ado, the jury hastily discharged him for fear he might attempt an explanation of the last casuality and kill some one else.
I do not think that the country has been edified by these laboured and clumsy attempts of the hon. gentleman opposite to explain away their defeat in Drummond-Arthabaska. The wound was so deep that government supporters have done little else *but talk about it since and make every effort to explain it away. But judging by what has transpired in the debate so far, what regrettable things may have been said by supporters of the Nationalist party in that election have been exceeded by prominent members of the party opposite, including cabinet ministers. For my part I can only say that, as regards any unpatriotic or unworthy statements made by speakers, whether on the side of the Nationalists or of the Liberal party, we entirely repudiate them and disassociate ourselves from any such expressions of opinion. But my right hon. friend the Prime Minister cannot complain of what has happened. He knows perfectly well that he and his own supporters sowed the seed of which these manifestations were the harvest. My right hon. friend is given to quote scripture occasionally. Let me recommend to him a text out of one of the minor prophets which says : 'They have sown the wind and they shall reap the whirlwind '. We are told that the Nationalists, in that campaign, fought against the idea of a more intimate union with the empire and preached a policy which involved abstention by Canada from all imperial
affairs. If that be so, I can only say that I entirely dissent from that view and am entirely convinced that those who hold it very greatly misunderstand the spirit and trend of the times. When in my district this summer, at Vernon, my right hon. friend declared that the Conservatives in the province of Quebec did not want to fight for England. I think that such a statement was hardly worthy of the right hon. gentleman. I do not want to press the tu quoque argument but I cannot help pointing out to the right hon. gentleman that he himself and his friends were not in the past very sound on this question. True, during this debate we have had some expressions of a desire on their part to fight anywhere and at all times for the British Empire. And to the extent to which the expression of that sentiment is sincere, from whatever side it comes, we may say that we have gained something from this storm of controversy. But it looks to me as if the right hon. gentleman, realizing that his party has become shattered and destroyed in the province of Quebec, is now going around and trying to capture the other provinces by making a strong imperial appeal to their sympathies.
The right hon. gentleman did the Conservatives of the province of Quebec rather scant justice in this matter, for if I understood my hon. friend from LCslet (Mr. Paquet) rightly, he closed his speech with these words :
We are willing to shed our Mood that Canada may he preserved to England. I will go even further; we are prepared to give up our blood in the conflicts of the empire, if only a majority of the Canadian people be ready for such a sacrifice.
This is a very noble sentiment. It is that if the people of Canada declare that they want to assist the empire the province of Quebec will do its share even to the shedding of the blood of its citizens in defence of that empire. I do not see what more the Prime Minister can want.
Let me say that in so far as the election in Drummond-Arthabaska was fought on the ground that the naval policy of the government should have been submitted to the country, I say that to that degree the defeat of the government candidate was a vindication of the best British constitutional practice.
The second proposition put before, this House again and again and before the country by hon. gentlemen opposite is that the policy of the Conservative party is a policy of cash contribution to Great Britain. After the clean cut, masterly and inspiring speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden)-a speech which constitutes an epoch in the history of this mat, ter, an utterance characterized by a spirit

of the highest statesmanship and most lofty patriotism-after such a speech one would have thought that we would have had no more misrepresentation along this line. But I notice that the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Fowke) again asserts that this was our policy and the right hon; the Prime Minister himself made a similar assertion this summer in my riding. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) down in the province of Quebec also declared that our policy was a direct cash contribution.
The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) also dwelt on this matter and said that if we had given this contribution we would have placed ourselves in an unfortunate position. That gentleman said some pleasant things about the amendment proposed by the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) last year; I only regret he could not have seen his way to say them at that time. The hon. gentleman's speech was in some ways one of the best we on this side of the House have listened to from hon. gentlemen opposite. It is true that the words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but from some passages that occurred in the speech it was quite evident that there was war in his heart.
The arguments that have been advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite against a contribution have constituted an attempt to prove the non-existence of any critical condition of imperial affairs at the present time, and to show that a contribution in money would be absolutely destructive of our autonomy. The hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Fowke) spoke of this crisis being due to the yellow press of England, a remark which I think is hardly in order. Nor will the protests of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) along the same line carry a great deal of weight. I shall quote one or two higher authorities than these gentlemen. One of the foremost living authorities on European affairs, Lord Rosebery, spoke these memorable words some months after the passage of the resolution of March, 1909:-
I do not know that in some ways I have ever seen a condition of things in Europe so remarkable, so peaceful, and in some respects so ominous, as the condition which exists at this moment. There is a hush in Europe, a hush in which one might almost hear a leaf fall to the ground. There is an absolute absence of any questions which ordinarily lead to war. . . . All, then, for bodes peace, and yet, at the same time, combined with this total absence of all questions of friction, there never was, in the history of the world, so threatening and overpowering a preparation for war. That is the sign which I regard as most ominous.
It was not therefore a crisis of the moment but a critical condition of affairs Mr. BURRELL.
which might extend over a period of several years that we on our side of the House designed to meet, a period during which gigantic and ominous preparations were and are being made. Can any man in this House, can any man in his senses say that we of the great Dominion would not have been justified in rendering assistance to Great Britain that was real assistance? The moral effect of it would have been incalculable and the result of it would have been that Canada, the greatest Dominion of the empire, would have been represented by two fighting vessels of the first-class instead of by paper cruisers, cruisers for the construction of which tenders have not yet been called. Those who talk autonomy, those who labour this word, and the dangers of losing autonomy, have a strangely limited conception of what the empire is. Why ^ should such action as we proposed impair our autonomy? I pointed out last year that if we contributed two battleships to_ Great Britain, these battleshins would still be in a real sense our battleships.
Let me quote the words of another great English statesman on this particular idea. The Hon. Alfred Lyttelton, used these memorable words:-
I quite agree that money contribution is an admirable way, but in my opinion it is not the best way to assist, yet it is very often the only way in which assistance can be given. I do not think that it contains in itself the slightest reflection upon autonomy-not the slightest; it is often the expression of the best way that the Dominion has of giving the assistance ... A good way to resist such an attack is to make the contribution take not the form of an annual grant, but a grant of such a sum of money as will build a ship, which will make a nucleus for effort and aspirations in the future, for the officering and ultimately even for the commanding of the ship by the citizens who have found her. And if I may be allowed to say a few words more, may I observe that whatever great dominions offers the imperial government a ship, I believe it is the case that that ship cannot be built or equipped in the dominion from which it proceeds, that it cannot at present be manned or officered effectively in the dominion from which it proceeds. My suggestion, therefore, is that the ship take her position as an equal amongst all the ships of His Majesty's navy; that she should be named, say after the colony, or after the dominion, which has found her; that the aspirations should be that she should be manned and officered ultimately by the citizens of the dominion, and so that she should not be of merely great and important assistance, but that she should be an objective, an aspiration for the national and martial feelings of the dominion which has shown such generosity.
The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) last year laboured this question of autonomy and his supporters followed suit. One would have thought we were back in the reign of George the Third to hear these

gentlemen, and that our self-government, our freedom, was being wrested from us by some violent attempts on the part of British statesmen. I do not think any gentlemen opposite will contradict the assertion that, there is not a responsible statesman on either side of politics in Great Britain to-day who does not rejoice in our freedom and in the full control that we have over our public affairs. They know that this freedom-and here I am quoting from Mr. Asquith, the leader of the present Liberal government,-that this freedom, allied to an ever-growing sense of unity, constitutes the secret and the safeguard of the empire itself.
It is to be hoped that there will be no more misrepresentation along this line, because there have been many misrepresentations up and down the country, largely I think the result of ignorance as to what Conservatives have said, as to what their position means. Only the other day the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) built up a superstructure of that kind, as was pointed out by the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). It is to be assumed that he did this out of ignorance as it would not be right to assume that he did it knowingly. Others who have misrepresented us have evidently done so through not being familiar with our programme.	.
Another fundamental difference between the government policy and our policy was forcibly pointed out by the leader of the opposition when he referred to the necessity of central control as making for the supremacy of the imperial government in time of war. One navy, said the leader of the opposition, with co-operating fleets which would co-operate, not fleets which might or might not co-operate according to the will of the government, because we have had the Prime Minister's own words that in such a war as the Crimean war he would not agree that the Canadian navy should take part and we have had remarks of that kind, and we have had strong efforts put forth in constituencies in Que-^ by supporters of the government, to show that the chances are that nothing would be able to force this Canadian navv into war for Great Britain.	'
[DOT] ,Mr.'McKenna, the First Lord of the British Admiralty urged the necessity of recog-nizmg_ the navy as imperial and not local. Me said:-
The navy problem of defence is one and the same the world over, and the maintenance of the supremacy at sea is the maintenance of supremacy in all the seas alike.
Sir, on June 7 of last year, Lord Rosebery in that speech to which I have already referred, a speech on imperial brotherhood, preceded by the playing by massed bands of The Maple Leaf, the Song of Australia,
and Rule Britannia, a speech which it is said could have been made by no other living man, described what the visitors' from the Dominions would see, and he closed with these words: ' And, last of all, surrounding all, and guarding it you will see a prodigious Armada, a prodigious, but always inadequate Armada. All of these are yours as much as ours. Your possessions, your pride !'
It is futile for the hon. gentleman opposite to say we had accepted the government position and had then gone back on it. It is idle for Nationalists to stamp the proposals as similar. Our complaint is that, having passed a resolution approving imperial defence in close co-operation with the imperial authorities, this government did not follow the admiralty suggestions and advice, advice resulting from long and ripe experience with large naval problems. My hon. friend the member for Red Deer supports the government policy because he finds it universally acclaimed in Great Britain. Expert opinion has by no means given -unqualified approval, but my hon. friend is not so foolish as not to know that his statement stands for nothing. Nobody knows better than he that any step we took however halting, would be welcomed and approved by public men in Great Britain. What has Mr. McKenna said?
If any dominions came to the admiralty at home, here and asked ns what our view was as to the best assistance for the purpose of a common defence which may be rendered, we should be ready with the answer, but we should not necessarily expect you to accept our answer. .	. . We will
assist in every way in our power, and whatever be the method by which we are asked to assist.
That is the case, the British Admiralty have assisted in the way they were asked to assist by this government. It is true that we may learn much from our own mistakes, but some mistakes are too costly and it is because we believe the government policy to be a mistake that we condemn it, and we take the solid ground that on so complicated a matter as a permanent policy the nation has a right to be heard and the refusal to grant this right is the rock on which the government will split. The British navy is our pride. More than ours, and I call the attention of the House to that fine tribute paid by the distinguished American who addressed the Canadian Club in this city on Saturday. ' Every man, woman and child should know it in his heart that the most important institution in the world to-day for human peace and justice, and maintaining of the great highways of trade is the British navy.'
' Your navy,' says Lord Rosebery. 'Your possession your pride,' and the answer of

the Prime Minister goes back, ' I am not an imperialist, I am not an anti-imperialist, I am for Canada first, last and all the time, and we are starting a navy of our own.'
'This British navy is your navy,' says Britain.'
' Certainly,' says the Prime Minister, ' What is yours is ours, and what is ours is our own.'
Mr. Speaker, permit me to point out the absolute failure of the government to follow out the best traditions of constitutional practice in this matter. In modern parliamentary government, 1784 marks the first time in which it was clearly recognized that the people were to be the great factor in public affairs. Mr. Pitt, who had remained in power in spite of hostile majorities in the House, advised dissolution, was granted it, and was sustained by the country. In regard to this Lord John Russell in his ' Memorials of Fox,' says:
The precedent of 1781, therefore, established this rule of conduct, that if the ministers chosen by the Crown do not possess the confidence of the House of Commons they may advise an appeal to the people, with whom rests the ultimate decision.
Later parliamentary practice in Great Britain, and elsewhere in the empire, has always, as we know, followed this precedent, and it stamps our form of government as being more strictly representative than that of one, like the United States foi instance, which has a fixed term.
But, Sir, there is much more than this. It may happen that although an administration is not defeated in the House its strength may have waned; popular opinion may have so changed, especially as some question or other of grave national importance has arisen, as to render it advisable to ascertain the true feeling of the country and enable the people to express it by a renewal, or a refusal of their confidence in the government. It is this phase of our constitutional practice which does in very truth make it essentially a government by the people, and it is the ignoring of this which stamps a government as autocratic and not democratic. My hon. friend the member for Red Deer, who is well versed in the political history of Great Britain may wish me to cite cases, and 1 will do so, and I trust that he, who so loudly and so constantly shouts for freedom with a big F, and for the right of the people to govern themselves, will re-examine himself, and see if his attitude of last year, and again this year, is not at strange variance with his political theories and convictions.
But, Mr. Speaker, we have a new Daniel come to judgment, a new interpreter of constitutional practice, a new exponent of parliamentary methods-the Minister of Marine and Fisheries-and I propose for a Mr. BURRELL.
moment or two to examine the extraordinary doctrines laid down for the House's edification in the minister's speech of last Wednesday.
It is a little difficult to summarize the minister's arguments very clearly because he has confused the whole matter by assuming that it was a plebiscite, and not a general appeal to the country, which was under discussion. It seems to me the minister must have done this purposely-I am of course open to correction-but, if not, purposely, then with so great ignorance of the facts as to make his position equally inexcusable. The member for Jacques Cartier clearly speaks of a general appeal, and not a plebiscite, in his amendment, and in any case the minister must have known perfectly well that it was an appeal to the people by a general election that the leader of the opposition emphatically urged last year. I agree with the minister that some questions are so complex that it would be difficult in adopting the plebiscite to so frame the question that a plain yes or no would answer it. Honourable gentlemen who think they can, would do well to recall that story of the celebrated Bi-adlaugh who refused to answer a question in public debate on the ground that he could not say yes or no. He was taunted by his opponent who said: * Why, certainly, you can answer any question you like by plain yes or no.' Mr. Bradlaugh asked him then if he had given up beating his wife? Honourable gentlemen will see the predicament he would he in if he had said either yes or no. There are some cases in which a plebiscite might be efficacious but certainly not such a one as the House is now discussing. Now, Sir, what does the minister say in Hansard, at page 168? These are the remarks of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries:
But, Sir, the fact is that the referendum or plebiscite is not in harmony with British constitutional practice. We have responsible government, we have a government of the people by the people, and if the government fails in its duty it may be overthrown to-morrow and a new government put in its place.
I take it that the reference is to the House of Commons.
In the United States the constitutional practice is different, because there the president and the congress is elected for a determined and a fixed period and it is their policy in some instances to submit important questions to the vote of the people. But, under the British system of parliamentary government the plebiscite is not in accordance with the constitutional practice and consequently it is not appealed to. And in addition to that, in my opinion it is very much better that the judgment of the people should be taken on such questions when the elections come on and then we will know exactly where we stand.

It will be observed how limited is the minister's conception of true, popular representative government. The people may express their will, he says, either when the ministry is defeated in the House of Commons-an unlikely thing in this country, where we are prone to stick hard and fast to party, or ' when elections come on '- ' come on ' certainly meaning at the expiration of the parliament's term. This is had enough, but later on the minister puts himself in a much worse position, and I could wish that my hon. friend from Red Deer {Mr. Clark), who has been promoted to the fifth bench on that side of the House, could have moved down to the third, behind the minister, and could have advised him on these high matters before the minister so hopelessly committed himself to unfortunate positions and pronouncements.
Let me refer now for a moment to British examples-I must heartily apologize to the House for taking so much time, and I too may he accused of threshing out old straw, but my conviction that the people's right of consultation has been flagrantly disregarded in this whole matter is so strong that I hope I shall have the pardon of the House in an endeavour to make our position perfectly clear.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister may remember that on Pitt's death Lord Grenville, in January, 1806, formed a coalition government, known as ' The Ministry of all the Talents.' Fox, who had come round to the opinion that it was necessary to prosecute the war with France with increased vigour, was a prominent member of the cabinet. Nine months after the ministry had taken office, Grenville resolved to appeal to the country. There had been no defeat of the government in the House, which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries seems to think even yet is the only justification for an appeal to the people. Fox had died recently; some doubts were felt by the government as to whether the people endorsed their attitude in regard to foreign affairs, and the Prime Minister determined to submit a question which profoundly affected the nation to that supreme arbiter-the popular will. There were many who thought no sufficient reason existed for dissolution, there were those who preached the doctrine advanced by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, viz., that these things should wait, as he put it the other day,
' until elections come on.'
In advising dissolution, Lord Grenville used these words:-
Fyr myself, sacred as I hold every prerogative of the Crown, I feel that His Majesty's servants are answerable for the advice which they give His Majesty for the exercise, or for abstaining from the exercise, of every one of them.
He defended his action by saying-and I 11
[DOT]*
am giving a brief digest of his argument as reported in the Parliamentary Debates-that if at any moment of history the exercise of the prerogative was wise and proper it was upon this occasion. He urged that the empire had gained immeasurably by the unanimity expressed by the people in regard to the vigorous prosecution of the war, and by their approbation of the steps taken by His Majesty's ministers.
Thus, Mr. Speaker, as in 1784, the doctrine had been clearly laid down that a government must appeal to the people when defeated in the Commons, so, in 1806, the further practice was established that on matters of grave national import a government was justified in appealing to the country, though no defeat of their policy had been sustained in the House. I particularly commend this to the consideration of the right hon. gentleman who leads this House, for he prides himself on his love of democracy and in his careful following of the practices of the mother of parliaments.
But, Sir, I might cite an equally strong case, and one which is being conducted at the present time before the eyes of all men. A Liberal government in Great Britain after a tenure of office similar in point of time to that of Lord Grenville's, has decided to make its appeal to the country. Lord Grewe states emphatically that dissolution is not the result of a breakdown of the conference, ' but-' and I use his own words.
But of the fundamental disagreement which is known, not merely to the eight men, but to all persons in a prominent position in either party.
We all know that the veto power of the Lords was freely discussed at the last general election though the budget may have been the main issue, but Lord Crewe added:
I doubt if there is any guarantee that the Lords will pay any attention to government views if they discuss either the power, or the reform of the House of Lords in this parliament. The circumstances justify us in appealing to the verdict of the country- and by the verdict of the country given at a general election, we are content to abide.
Well, Sir, as in 1806, so in 1910, there are those who think dissolution an abuse of the prerogative of the Crown by the ministers. My right hon. friend's former supporter, and latterly his bitter critic, Mr. Joseph Martin, denounces dissolution as absolutely unjustified. Lord Lansdowne points out that the government has received no parliamentary check, and that such a course was ousting parliament from a proper opportunity of discussing a question which the government had promised full discussion of when the Bill to which the veto-resolutions were only a preliminary, was introduced. I am not going into the question of whether that dissolution was or was not justified,



and I am not foolish enough to think this House would care a rap as to my particular views, but I desire to emphasize the point that here is a Liberal government in Great Britain going to the country after less than a year's tenure of office, having received no defeats in the House. Why? Confessedly to obtain the verdict of the country on a great question which, though partially discussed, was still a question on which they had received no clear mandate from the people.
Mr. Speaker, I have endeavoured to give a fair presentation of the facts connected with constitutional practice, and I now ask the Prime Minister in the light of these facts where he and his government stand at the present time in the eyes of the people? He will not deny that so tremendous a step as the creation of a costly navy in this country is not a fit matter for the people to give their mandate on.
He will not deny,-he dare not deny-that so short a time ago as in 1907 he flatly refused to support a general scheme of imperial defence. He will not dare to urge that in the general elections of 1908 the question was made in any degree or measure whatsoever a question for popular discussion, for approval or disapproval by the people. But in spite of that failure to seek or obtain a mandate he does what no responsible minister in the mother of parliaments has ever done, or would ever do. He admits in his letter to ' La Presse ' on November 17, that there is a misunderstanding in the country as to the naval policy-but he persists in declining to hear the verdict of the people-I leave Jt to the judgment of this House whether I am not right in insisting that this government is autocratic and not democratic in its character and practice?
What does the Prime Minister say in that letter to ' La Presse ' to which I have referred?
I know that in the country districts a false idea has been spread of the navy which, in concert with my colleagues of the cabinet, and the majority of the Houses, I have undertaken to create.
' I '-not the people-I, with the assistance of my majorities in the Houses-supporters too many of whom wear that collar to which the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) referred. ' I ' have created. This is the colossal egotism-this is the ar-rogation of supreme authority which invariably precedes the debacle ! Canadians, who years and years ago entered into their inheritance of freedom and self-government, are startled by hearing a new doctrine announced by the Prime Minister-the doctrine of ' government of the people and for the people '! That last vital portion of the older democratic faith * by the people,' is eliminated in the new creed. Blind to a Mr. BL RRELL.
true vision of the present time, obstinate in the face of repeated warnings, my right hon. friend will realize these things only when the hour is too late to Vepair his irrevocable mistake.
Sir, before taking my seat, there is one matter in connection with the amendment and with this debate which it is necessary to touch very briefly. The hon. member for Red Deer finds a valid and sufficient reason for opposing the amendment in the confusion which would result in the country if the amendment carried. Ho says (' Hansard,' p. 311):-
The only outcome of the carrying of the resolution would he the precipation of a general election, and X want to ask my hon. friend who occupies the responsible position of leader of the opposition if he thinks it would tend to build up the empire or the Canadian nation that a general election should be precipitated on this delicate question of the foreign policy of the empire, and the imperial connection?
In answering that I must again direct my hon. friend to that modern constitutional authority-that modern substitute for Todd and May-the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. On page 168 of ' Hansard ' he says
But we are not afraid of the judgment of the people; on the contrary, we are in favour of consulting the people. There will be that consultation when the elections come on, and at that time the people will know exactly where they are. They will know, as they know to-day, the policy established by the government. They will know the policy of the Conservative party, generally speaking, because that party is in favour of a contribution.
Strange to say, a little later on the minister swallows his words, and in arguing against a plebiscite on the naval policy, says:-
That being the case, would it be advisable, on a question on which the issues are not well determined, a question on which the policy of either party is not fully understood, to take a vote of the people?
And finally he says:-
If, on appeal to the people, it be found that our policy does not accord with public opinion, the people will have the right to reverse that policy.
Sir, the grievous wrong which this government has inflicted on the people is that on this, as on that other question of the Grand Trunk Pacific, they have committed the country, tied the people hand and foot without their consent, and then, while unctuously stating that the people have a right to reverse that policy, have dared them to do so by shouting the ugly words ' repudiation,' ' breach of national faith,' or by lamenting, as my hon. friend from Red Deer does, the confusion which would ensue

if the government were defeated. By such an argument my hon. friend stultifies and condemns himself, for his failure to support an appeal last year before the country was committed, and offers the flimsiest of defences for the over-riding of popular rights. Sir, if the people condemned this government, which I believe they would do if appealed to, they could then, and would, safely entrust the solution of this great problem to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, resting assured that the national honour would be upheld, and national aspirations be realized.
Here, in my closing word, is the Conservative position, clearly defined and nobly expressed bv it3 leader:-
1.	Effective and immediate aid to the empire at any moment that the integrity- the safety-if that empire may be endangered or threatened.
2.	A policy of one central control in time of war as an essential factor in maintaining supremacy at sea.
3.	A firm belief that these two aims can be achieved, and are absolutely consistent with the fullest development of our liberties as a self-governing people.
4.	And lastly, that in the formulation of a great permanent naval policy, which so vitally affects the nation, the people have an absolute and indisputable right to be consulted.
This, Mr. Speaker, is our position, this our confession of faith, and this it is which gives me at once justification and pleasure in voting for the amendment of the leader of the opposition.

I do not propose to follow the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) to any extent. I think hon. members will agree with me that the hon. gentleman's speech has the face of a familiar friend, and is of a familiar flavour. I give the hon. member (Mr. Burrell) the credit for having in perhaps some parts of it committed it to memory a little better than he did last year, but so far as I have been able to follow his arguments they appear to me to be a sort of resume of those which he put forth last year in favour of the peculiar position of the opposition on the question of the establishment of a Canadian navy. Now, Sir, it is not my intention to discuss at any great length the amendments which have been placed before the House by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) and by the hon. the leader of the opposition, because it seems to me that so far as discussion on the floor of the House goes, enough time has already been taken up this session and last in placing before the people of Canada the various views held by different members of this House on the question of Canada's policy in the matter of national defence, lit
We on the government side do not need to reiterate or explain our position, for our position has been consistent from the introduction of this question of national defence in this parliament until now. By common consent in this House a resolution was adopted in March, 1909, which appears to place this important subject outside the realm of partisan discussion. On the motion of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), and subsequent amendment of that motion, it was unanimously declared by this House that there devolved upon this parliament of Canada the duty of providing for our own national defence upon the sea. That question seemed to have been satisfactorily settled on that occasion. But, when the leader of the government introduced his Naval Bill, which was so fully discussed last year, the members on the government side of the House found to their very great surprise, that the leader of the opposition and his followers had taken another view of the situation-or, as an hon. friend near me suggests, other views. They no longer felt in duty bound to support the declarations to which they had given their unanimous consent less than twelve months before. My hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) may argue this question till he is black in the face, and so .may hon. members on that side, but they will not be able to convince the great mass of the people that the Conservative party has not broken their faith and gone back on the pledge which they gave to the people in their support of the resolution of March, 1909. As the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo devoted so much time to quotations from constitutional authorities on these important matters, I would have liked him to cite a case in the history of any civilized nation in which the question of national defence was put before the people in the form of a plebiscite.

I am not a lawyer and am not accustomed to splitting hairs ; I look at this question and the attitude of hon. members opposite toward it as the people of this country generally regard it and as they will regard it when they decide by their vote as between the parties on this question. I contend that this question of national defence is outside the realm of plebiscite or referendum, from the very fact that it is a duty devolving upon the government of any self-governing colony and any civilized country. There is, to my mind, no reason whatever why this question should be referred to the people, either by plebiscite or any other means, except, of course, in the usual way. The people of this country will have an opportunity, at the next general election, to say whether or not they are content with the naval policy of the government, and I venture to say that that will be quite soon enough for hon. gentlemen opposite. I simply wish to point out to the House again, and to emphasize, the equivocal position of the opposition in this House on this great question. They tell us that they have never receded from their position in 1909. Why, Sir, that is a preposterous notion, when we have before us the resolution of 1909, and the speeches of the leader of the opposition in the summer of that year explicitly declaring in favour of a Canadian navy. It is quite beyond my comprehension how hon. gentlemen Mr. NEELY.
opposite can expect the people of this country to believe that they have taken a consistent course on this naval question since it came before this House.
Now, as I said when I arose, it is not my intention to discuss at any length the various views taken by hon. gentlemen on the other side on this question ; nor is it my intention to discuss the amendments before the House, because there are other matters in connection with the speech from the Throne, to which, I think, as a western man, it is my duty to give some small attention.
In his address in reply to the mover of the address, the leader of the opposition saw fit to make reference to a number of questions of moment, questions that are pressing upon the minds of a great majority of the people of the west. And he turned to his followers from the western provinces as if to throw them some little sop of comfort as to his attitude towards the people of the west and the questions that are at present agitating the minds _ of those people. One of the questions which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) discussed was the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. We all know that the construction of the railway is of vital moment to the people of western Canada. We are also convinced in the west that it is of great importance to eastern Canada. I cannot conceive that such a great undertaking, which is bound to benefit so directly and largely the people of western Canada, can in any way work detrimentally to the interest of the east. Still it was with considerable satisfaction that I heard the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) state explicitly that the two great parties were agreed on this point, that the construction of the Hudson Bay railway was an imperative necessity. That statement is a matter of some satisfaction to the people of the west. We all know that it is the fondest ambition of the leader of the opposition to occupy some day the seat now filled by the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and I am glad indeed to know in advance that if the hon. gentleman should ever attain the position-and I trust that the day when he will do so is still far distant-I am glad to know that he will then be in a frame of mind which will enable him to realize the great needs arising out of the growing prosperity and the growing population of our great prairie provinces. There is only one thing I am afraid of in connection with the statement of' my hon. friend the leader of the opposition on this question, and that is that when the Hudson Bay railway scheme is submitted, the hon. gentleman will find himself in the same position as he did when we came to discuss the Navy Bill.

The policy of constructing the Hudson Bay railway will be all right, but the government proposal will be so absolutely wrong that no railway at all will be better than one built as the government propose to build it. That no doubt will be the conclusion arrived at by the hon. gentleman. But whether or not the hon. gentleman be to-day in favour of the Hudson Bay railway scheme, I want to assure him that wdrenever that railway is actually completed and in operation-as it will be very soon-none of the credit will belong in any sense to the leader of the opposition. Let me remind the House that the construction of this road was a part of the Liberal platform at the last general election, and the time, the place and the circumstances in which the leader of the government made the announcement of his policy to build that road are evidence of his sincerity of purpose. I had many times looked over the various planks in the platform upon which the Conservative party appealed to the people at the last general election, and I have failed to find out one reference to this great undertaking.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), for some reason or another, has but recently become alive to that fact that there is a territory in the Dominion, west of Lake Superior. No doubt some of his friends from the west have been giving him a little education on this subject. This past summer we had the honour in western Canada of a visit from the right hon. the leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the hon. the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham). 1 have noticed a disposition on the part oi certain western Conservative members to rush into print with statements to the effect that, in so far as the political value of that western tour was concerned, it all redounded to the benefit of the opposition.

My hon. friend says hear, hear. If that be the conclusion of these hon. gentlemen, why should they have deemed it necessary to rush into print in order to make public what to them appeared so self-evident. We out west were glad to have that visit from the first citizen of Canada. We were glad if only for the reason that no matter what party may be in power, that party must recognize the fact that the west is developing very rapidly and that our rulers must visit that country frequently in order to keep in touch with its marvellous progress. I am rather inclined to think that these references to western questions made by the hon. the leader of the opposition were due to the visit of the right hon. gentleman and his Minister of Railways to our prairie provinces this year, and I am very glad indeed that we have this tardy recognition on the part of the leader of the opposition. It is not my intention to discuss any particular plan or scheme which the government may adopt regarding this Hudson Bay railway, because that would be speaking in advance of a measure not yet submitted to us, but let me say this that the opposition to that railway, shown in certain quarters in some of the eastern provinces, is absolutely unfounded. We in the west believe in the necessity for this railway, first of all as a colonization road. In that part of the country to be opened by it we believe there are unlimited resources of various kinds as yet practically untouched by the hand of man. I have been looking through the reports of the engineers who have been surveying the route, and I find that some of them speak in very glowing terms indeed of the territory through which this road will pass. In fisheries, minerals, agricultural lands and particularly in timber, the district will be found an exceedingly profitable one to develop, and exceedingly profitable for the operation of a railway. So that, if only as a colonization road, it is the duty of this government to carry out this project at the earliest possible date. Certain engineers have this summer been looking up the water-powers, and one of them, Mr. Ogilvie, in a recent interview, made the statement that nowhere in Canada could more valuable water-powers be developed at less cost than at the Nelson River rapids. I think he said for instance that the chief rapids of the Nelson river would furnish in the neighbourhood of
1,000,000 horse-power at very small cost, so that at least a portion of the railway could be operated from these immense water-powers if it should be found too expensive to operate them by steam. The Hudson Bay railway would be a disappointment to the people of the west if it were not more than a successful colonization railway, because the thought of the western people is centred in the idea that that road will form a new transportation route to the markets of the world which will have a very marked effect in lessening the cost of marketing their products. 1 know there is a variety of opinions as to whether the route is practicable for transportation purposes. I have looked up a number of authorities and find that they differ on this point very widely. There are those who state that the straits entering into Hudson Bay are navigable all the year round, and there are others who confine the navigability of the straits to the months of July, August, September and part of October, but in any case I am convinced that this route will prove at least a safety valve in the transportation problem of the west, it will alleviate those congested conditions which have occurred

a32
in the past few years and that are very likely, notwithstanding the extensive railroad development that is taking place in the west to recur in the near future; it will be an alternative route if nothing else. I do not mean to say that the Hudson Bay route will divert all western trade to the markets of the world to itself, but I contend it will have an enormous effect in regulating the freight rates on other roads, on both our imports and our exports.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has again introduced to this House and to the people, the old question, threshed out so industriously and so thoroughly some four years ago, when the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were given their autonomy, as to whether or not the prairie provinces should have the control of their lands. There is some measure of consistency in his position on this question, because in the platform on which he appealed to the people of this country at the last election he made some reference to this question, one of his planks being:-
That the public lands be restored to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan upon fair terms.
I need not discuss that question at length because the people of those two provinces have already pronounced twice as to whether or not they are satisfied with the financial terms of the Autonomy Bills and their verdict in both cases has been in the affirmative. But perhaps my hon. friend is not as kind to the western provinces as his words would imply. It is merely a matter of opinion -whether the western provinces should have the control of the public lands in these provinces, or whether they should, as at present, obtain subsidies in lieu of those lands. One thing is clear to my mind, that the policy already adopted by this government of retaining those lands for settlement purposes, for distribution as free homesteads to the people who go there from other provinces in Canada or from other countries, is undoubtedly the policy best adapted to the growth and development of western Canada.
I would like to know exactly what the leader of the opposition means by this proposition to give the western provinces their lands. The statement in his platform that these lands should be restored to the provinces, has a tale attached in the words ' upon fair terms.' That plank is something like the hon. gentleman's position on the tariff. He tells us he is in favour of adequate protection and the great trouble is to ascertain what adequate protection means.

speechtext:
And the people in the west, when they came in 1908 to consider this plank in his platform, were at a loss to understand what he meant by the expression ' restore the public lands on fair terms,' ' What are these fair terms? Are they terms that would bind the western provinces to a colonization policy, or a homestead policy like the policy of the present administration of the Interior Department? If that were the case where would those provinces find a revenue? Where would they derive -a revenue if they had no subsidies in lieu of those lands? The subsidy which they now receive is being utilized to improve the roads and bridges throughout the provinces. If the subsidy were taken away and the lands were given to the provinces, it follows, as night' follows the day, that these provinces would be comjrelled to use these lands not for purposes of distribution as free homesteads, but to sell them to the highest bidder in order to get a revenue to carry on the affairs of the provinces. So, when the leader, of the opposition touches this subject again, I would be very very glad indeed to know just what he means by this particular part of his programme.
The hon. gentleman says also that there is an urgent demand in the west for a lower tariff on agricultural implements. As reported in ' Hansard,' he said:-[DOT]
But the farmers of the west say something more. They say there ought to be lower duties on agricultural implements, that they are paying higher prices for implements than are paid in the United States and higher prices for Canadian implements than these implements are sold for abroad. I say the government is derelict in its duty in not having brought down to parliament direct and positive information on this subject, and I say that if the claims that are made are true there ought to be a remedy. And I want to know from the government whether they believe them to be true or not. If they say that they do not know, I ask why they have not taken means to know; if they say that these claims are not true, I ask upon what evidence they base that assertion and what they propose to do in the premises.
If you can get anything more beautifully indefinite than that statement on this question as an announcement of policy as or committing the leader of the opposition to any definite policy on this subject, I would like to know w'here it is to be found in the history of the English language. The hon. gentleman wants to know what the government think about the tariff and lowering the duties on agricultural implements. But I want to know what about that hon. gentleman himself who has a responsibility to the people of this country as well as the members of this government. Some three years ago this matter was discussed fully in

the House, and the House was fully seized of this demand of the western farmers follower duties on agricultural implements. If I read his statement correctly, the leader of the opposition on that occasion voted against that resolution; not only did he vote against it, but he made a speech in which he practically acknowledged himself unconvinced of the necessity of making that reduction. Now he appeals to the government to know what they are going to do. I think that is a little bit of heroics on the part of the leader of the opposition that will not deceive any member of this House, or anybody in this country. The hon. gentleman also asked certain questions as to what the government proposes to do to remedy the conditions of the grain trade in western Canada. We have in the speech from the Throne a reference to certain proposed legislation dealing with terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, and the leader of the opposition makes some reference to that important question. He said:
The west asks also the redress of grievances in the operation of terminal elevators. They declare that the farmers of the west are shamelessly robbed through these elevators, that ten per cent of No. 1 wheat goes in and thirty per cent goes out, and so on all along the line. They declare that this condition of affairs has existed to the knowledge of the government for many years and without redress.
Now if the hon. gentleman were in his seat 1 would like to ask him a question. Does he consider that this administration has done nothing in the interest of the farmers of the west in improving the conditions of the grain trade? Why, Sir, to-day any man from the west knows that the conditions of the grain trade are one hundred per cent better than they were, even ten or twelve years ago. A great many reforms have been worked out by this government that were never thought of by the previous administration. When this government came into power the grain trade of the west was in a very unsatisfactory position, the people were in the grasp of monopolists, and practically the farmers had to ship every bushel of wheat through the initial elevator owned by private concerns, and to accept whatever price they chose to give. The introduction of loading platforms at every way station and every flag station on our western railroads has broken up that monopoly. The Manitoba. Grain Act and the Sale and Inspection Act have brought about great advantages in the grain trade. I want to say that the only serious complaint the farmers have to-day is in reference to the manipulation of grades at the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur. I am free to say, however, speaking tor myself, for my constituents, and I believe for the people of the west generally, so far as I know their opinions, that some remedy is necessary for this condition of affairs, and I would say to the members of the government who may have this matter in charge that in any measure which they may bring before the House they should be satisfied beyond question, before introducing the measure, that it will be effective in stopping these abuses that have existed for so long at the terminal elevators.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it might appear to some persons that my remarks, dealing so largely with western questions, are somewhat of a sectional nature. I do not wish them to be interpreted in that way. I consider that the prosperity of the east and the prosperity of the west are bound together so closely that what adds to the prosperity of western Canada must necessarily add to the industrial prosperity of eastern Canada. For that reason I am making this appeal to the people of the east to give sympathetic consideration to these questions I have just discussed, because, while it may be true that some of these measures affect the people of the west more particularly^ the government which carries out these projects of reform will confer an inestimable benefit upon all the people of Canada.
