In continuing this debate I do not propose to take up much time of the House. First, of all, I wish to congratulate the hon. gentleman (Mr. McGiverin) who fnoved the address in reply to the speech from the Throne, upon the admirable way in which he performed his task. It was certainly creditable to him, and I am sure was pleasing to the House. As to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lapointe) who seconded the address, I am in the position of my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) in that I have not yet been able to read that hon. gentleman's speech, and therefore cannot appreciate it as I probably otherwise would.
The debate that has occurred on the Address has been largely confined to two questions, the navy and a reciprocity treaty with the United States. The hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Neely) seemed very anxious to know what attitude the Conservative party were going to take with reference to those two questions. He started out by arguing that the Conservative party were in favour of a plebiscite. Now the hon. gentleman must have been in this House last session, and he must be aware of the fact that the Conservative party voted almost unanimously against the proposal for a plebiscite on this question; therefore it was a waste of time for him to argue that the Conservative party were wrong in supporting a plebiscite, because in fact they were opposed to it. Next, he wanted to know the reason why this ques-

tion should be submitted to the people either by a plebiscite or otherwise. He was quite satisfied with that at least. There was no reason why it should be submitted to the people until the general election comes on. That is just exactly the position taken by the right hon. the leader of the government. We claim that that conduct is arbitrary, autocratic, tyrannical and out of harmony with the principles of constitutional government as carried out both in the imperial parliament and in the colonial dependencies of the British Empire. There is no better understood principle in legislation and in party government in the British Empire than that any great and important question, before the country is committed to it, should be submitted to the people for their approval or for their voice. But what have we to-day? Is it government by the people and for the people? Is it government by the people if those who are charged with the responsibility of the administration of the people's affairs first do the act and then consult the people after the act. is done, never giving them an opportunity to express their voice upon it before they are committed to the act and must bear the consequences of it whether they are good or bad? That is not government by the people. It may be, in the estimation of some, government for the people, but it is not government by the people, nor is it domocratic government notwithstanding the fact that the right hon. gentleman has always claimed that he is the representative of the democratic principle. Yet, the hon. member for Humboldt says there is no reason in the world why it should be submitted to the people. His leader said the same. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries-I was going to say marine and navy-says exactly the same. Well, I say that is autocratic, I say that is over-bearing, I say that is ignoring the people's common and well-understood right-the right of saying whether or not they approve of this being done before they are committed to it and before the country has carried it out for a number of years.
The hon. member for Humboldt goe?s on to speak of the construction of the Hudson Bay railway and says that it is very much needed. What is the policy of the leader of the opposition on this question? Well, the leader of the opposition is not charged with the responsibility of building it. He could not build it if he desired; he could not spend a dollar on such an undertaking. Ought the hon. member not rather to be very much more concerned as to what is the policy of the leader of the government on that question and try to get him pinned down to some policy in the interest of the great western country which he seems to be so anxious to represent in this House today? It seems to me, in all fairness, that Mr. SPROULE.
he should feel very much greater concern about the men who have the power to build or refrain from building this' road than he does about the leader of the opposition and his supporters who could not commence that undertaking nor spend a dollar on it no matter how worthy it was.
Now, I would like to direct attention to one other thing as well. It is so very much needed, the hon. member says, and it is patent to every person, not only people living in that country, but people who are at all acquainted with the growth and histor.y of that country. It must be patent to them. They must appreciate the importance of building that road. I assume that the right hon. the leader of the government must have known that fourteen years ago and known it all the time from that up to the present. Surely his friends think that they have had the power to do the work necessary to help the people there; yet, what have they done in all these lourteen years? How much of that road have they built? What have they done with regard to it? Knowing, as they must have known, howf desirable it was in the interest of the development of the country that it should be built? Why, for the first time, they are commencing to build a bridge that may or may not be in the future a portion of the road. That is all they have done, all they have committed themselves to-the building of a bridge at the Pas Mission. They are going to build a bridge across the river there. They are commencing it. If it takes them as long to build that bridge, and if they are as successful in the construction of it as they have been with regard to the Quebec bridge then I can only say that all my sympathy is for the western people, because it will be a long time before they can utilize it in running cars for the Hudson Bav railway.
The hon. member for Humboldt said something about the people of the prairie provinces. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition said that if he were entrusted with the administration of the government of this country the people of the prairie provinces would get their land back on fair terms. The hon. member for Humboldt objects to that. He wants to know what that means. Does not the merest tyro in this House know what fair terms means? Can he not, as a western man, compare the difference between what would be fair and unfair? Does he not know what will be fair terms? I should think so, and I should think that not only he, but his western friends as well ought to be amply satisfied with any government or party when they propose to give them back these lands and to give them back to them on fair terms. He says that he is not going to discuss the tariff on agricultural implements, but he wants to know what the leader of the oppo-

sition is going to do. Well, now, need I tell him that the leader of the opposition has no power to do anything?. Ought he not to be very much more interested in knowing what his friends are going to do, and very much more desirous of ascertaining what the leader of the government, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs are going to do, because they are the only ones who can change the tariff in any particular in regard to agricultural implements or any other article that the western people are so much interested in? He seems to have no faith in them. Evidently he has not.
I said that I did not intend to discuss this question at any very great length. But the debate has been confined largely, or principally, to two items in the speech from the Throne. The first of these has reference to the naval question. The second deals with the proposal of reciprocity with the United States. The motion now before the House deals with the naval question, and invites our attention more particularly to that subject. I wish to give a very few reasons why I intend to vote, as I propose to do, on this subject. There are two or three motions before the House, two by way of amendment to the speech from the Throne, the last, an amendment to the amendment, and I desire to give to the House some reasons for my voting as I propose to do on this question. It is because the principle involved is one of the basic principles of constitutional government, whether in Great Britain, in the Dominion of Canada, or under any other colonial government. The British parliament and the parliament of the colonial dependencies as well have a sacred Tegard for it has been one of the basic principles of constitutional government until they become autocratic, tyrannical, and neglect it, or refrain from standing by it, _ What is that principle? That principle involves consulting the people and allowing them to express their will on the subject before committing the country to the undertaking. We claim to be democratic in our instincts, our aims and purposes.
Under democratic government the people rule, and one of its basic principles is that they should be consulted before the die is cast in any important national undertaking. When Canada embarks on a naval policy which means a complete change in her policy in that respect, surely the people should have an opportunity to say whether they approve or disapprove. Such a policy means heavy expense in its initiation, constantly increasing expense in its maintenance, and the people have a right to say, whether they will undertake the burden to be cast upon them. Notwithstanding that this policy changes our relations with the mother country and the other dependencies of the
empire 'the Prime Minister of Canada is quite ready in his own autocratic fashion to plunge the country into the scheme to such an extent that it may not be possible to reverse the action which he has thus unconstitutionally taken. He tells us that he will be quite prepared to take the verdict of the people when the general elections come, but remember, that verdict will not be given until three years after the promulgation of the government's policy. I do not think the people of the Dominion will regard that as government by the people, for the people; I think they will regard it as the government by an autocrat and for an autocrat; I think they wrill regard it as the government of a tyrant. Under the British system as exemplified in Britain itself the people are consulted on any great policy. Gladstone was in favour of Home Rule for Ireland but he propounded his policy and submitted it to the people and the people pronounced against it. The present government of Great Britain on the question of the Lords veto are to-day taking the verdict of the people. The Rt. Hon. A. J. Balfour, the leader of the Conservative party has laid down the principle that this important question which the people of England are now facing should be submitted to a referendum, and he adds that he will be governed by the voice of the people thus as expressed. But, in Canada since this present government came into power they have dealt with important questions in the most autocratic fashion, and have belied their declarations that they were democrats to the hilt. They undertook the construction of the Yukon railway, which based on the value at which the mining land was then being sold by the government in that locality would cost $150,000,000 for an inferior railway 150 miles long; the cabinet if you please, undertook the building of that railway without ever letting the people know what they were about. I declared then that such conduct on the part of the government was high handed and autocratic and 1 declare so to-day. But, with regard to that project the government were rightly defeated in their object by the wisdom of the Senate of that day. Then, in regard to the Transcontinental railway, they declared that the project would revolutionize the transportation system of the Dominion and they lightly undertook it without consulting the people. They told the people that the surplus of one year, about $15,000,000, would do the whole trick, but now we know it will cost the people of Canada between $200,000,000 and $300,000,000. That fact must have been as well known to intelligent men then as it is now, but notwithstanding, the government, in a light hearted fashion committed the country to that huge expenditure without consulting the

people who have to provide the money. The whole history of the present Liberal government shows that they throw to the winds the principle of government by the people for the people. And, now in regard to the establishment of the Canadian navy which must inevitably change our relations to the mother country, there has been no effort to obtain the wishes of the people, and in all human probability the scheme proposed by the government would not be approved by the majority of the people of Canada if submitted to them in the form which the government has decided upon, and yet, these gentlemen on the treasury _ benches call their government a constitutional and a democratic government when in truth it is an autocratic government, a tyranical government, a government by the executive and not by the people.
I think it was the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) who challenged us to give a single instance of the Conservative party consulting the people. I will give him one. Did not the Conservative party lay down their policy before the election of 1878? Did not they lay down the National Policy and appeal to the people upon it? Was not that policy clearly declared, and did not the people express clear approval of it? They did. That was democratic government, government of the people by and for the people. And did not the Conservative party carry out that policy when entrusted with power? No one will deny that they did. I listened with great interest to the statement of the Prime Minister on reciprocity. He said that the National Policy was as dead as an Egyptian mummy- those, I believe, were his very words. The present government have no policy for the management of the nation about which they boast so much. Instead of the National Policy they have a haphazard, unbusinesslike policy intended to suit only, the exigencies of the party, or the whims of the individual, for the time being controlling the situation. I should think that for their own credit, they would be ashamed to make such an admission. If they regarded this as a country worth governing, much more if they regarded it as the noble nation the Prime Minister declares it to be, they would have some kind of policy suited for a nation. But the Prime Minister tells us that the National Policy is as dead as any Egyptian mummy. How did they kill it? Was it by amendment of the tariff, by repealing duties which are the essence of that policy? No; they did not change these in any particular. Let me ask them one question: Would they daTe to go to the manufacturers, the farmers. the industrial workers of this country, and declare to them that the Notional Policy was entirely repealed or that they were ready to repeal every part of it now in existence? No, they dare not do that. They Mr. SPROULE.
know that the farmers and all others in industrial life would turn that against them as one man. When the time comes for the First Minister to appeal to the people, let him dare say to the electors of Canada that he will repeal the National Policy, and I am inclined to think that they will give him an answer that will startle him out of his dream.
On the subject of the Canadian Pacific railway,, the Conservative party had regard to this question of constitutional democratic government by consulting the people on the question of how the road should be constructed. Their opponents said that the system should be part by rail and part by waterway. But the Conservative party declared for an all-rail route as their policy and submitted the question to the people; and their policy was endorsed.
I come now to the proposal for reciprocity with the United States. The Prime Minister twitted the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) because an appeal was made to the people on the question of reciprocity in 1891. That appeal was made, and what happened? The Conservatives were returned to power. Representatives were sent by that government to Washington, but they came back declaring their mission a failure. That was no discredit to them; they could not get the reciprocity they wanted, they would not accept what was offered, and they came back with no arrangement completed. But the point I wish to make is that their action in this matter also was in harmony with the principle of constitu-' tional government. Is the Prime Minister following this course in regard to reciprocity to-day? Not at all. He dare not submit that question to the people. If he did, I am inclined to think that a large majority of the people would tell him that they are not in favour of any kind of reciprocity that he is likely to get at this time. While saying this, I am not arguing either against reciprocity or for it; I am arguing in favour of the principle invariably followed by the Conservatives, and as invariably ignored or defied by their opponents, of appealing to the people on important questions of government. The Conservatives, to their credit be it said, have been willing to appeal to the people and to accept the people's verdict.
When asked to cite an instance of the party now in power appealing to the people on any great question of government, one hon. member on that side asked, did not they appeal to the people on the plebiscite on the liquor question? Yes, they did. And it was the only time when they appealed to the country people on any question asking the people's verdict. And what happened after the plebiscite was taken? Why, they did the same in that case as on the naval question-they ignored the will of the people. In that plebiscite a majority de-

dared for the abolition of the liquor traffic. But the government did not move hand or foot to implement that decision by any parliamentary enactment. They ignored the declaration of the people entirely. The Prime Minister said there was an understanding among their friends that, unless there was an overwhelming verdict in favour of prohibition they would not implement it by legislation. It must have been a secret understanding, and yet this was given as the reason why they refused to respect the people's will.
The question was asked in the course of the debate: Why were not the people consulted on the proposal of confederation? I think it was the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur). How could they consult the people, with no federal parliament in existence? They were trying then to bring about confederation. What would have been the result if appeals had been made by each province separately? The result would have been no confederation. Had there been a federal parliament to consult the people as a whole, no doubt .they would have been consulted and their verdict would have been respected. But some friends of the leader of the present government did consult the people on this question of confederation. The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), when at the head of a provincial government, appealed to the people on the question of secession. And with what result? Why, he acted in a manner perfectly consistent with that of his friends. He was in favour of secession and appealed to the people on that question. The people declared in his favour, but, although he was at the head of a government, he ignored the verdict of the people, evidently being afraid to carry it out. The record of the party now in power shows that they have always ignored the people's will in carrying out their policies. I have given you several examples that should prove the correctness of what I say.
But now we are dealing with the question of the construction of a navy. That is a question which formed the chief subject of controversy in the Drummond-Arthabas-ka election, and the result of that election has been the chief staple of debate on the opposite side. Well, the government did try to consult the people in a miniature of controversy in the Drummond-Arthabaska.	They selected their own battle ground, they carefully chose a constituency where it seemed utterly impossible that a verdict could be not against them, they went over the ground in advance, and the constituency was one which for thirty-five years had elected a supporter of the right hon. gentleman and his friends. What was the result? The people gave a verdict against the government and its policy, and now these hon. gentlemen are very much exercised and annoyed and are at their wits end
to show some reason for their defeat. I have listened to the whole of the debate, I have read the newspapers, I have looked over the whole situation, and to my mind the outcome is simply due to this fact. Ever since 1896 the government have appealed over and over again to the electors on lines of race and creed, but in the Drum-mond-Arthabaska election, they were met by adversaries who beat them at their own game and now they can do nothing but squeal. They are poor sportsmen who cannot take a licking like men but must go around whimpering over it. Now they say that the election was not fair, that it was won by the other party in the way in which the government themselves had gained many a victory in that province and in that constituency, for we must all admit that never in this House or out of it has there been a public man more successful in appealing to the people of Quebec along the lines of race and religion than the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur). In that respect the hon. gentleman is the greatest sinner in the Dominion to-day. The other day he taunted me with riding the Protestant horse. But I should like to know what horse he has been riding in Quebec over and over again? Has it not been the Roman Catholic horse and the French horse? Has he ever trusted to anything else in his appeals to the people. The hon. gentleman cannot point to any instance in which I ever mentioned the Protestant horse except when drawn out by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) or some of his friends. There is no one in this country who is more adept than the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brodeur) in bringing up these race and religious questions when he thinks he can get any political profit out of them. The verdict given at Drummond-Arthabas-ka, he says, was unfavourably obtained, the people were misled and deluded, and the verdict itself was a national calamity. Well, if my judgment be worth anything, it is a national calamity which could be repeated in seven out of every ten rural constituencies in Ontario to-day if an appeal were made to the people. If the electors of Drummond-Arthabaska are such great sinners because they gave the verdict they did, all I can say is that, should an appeal be made to the electors, it will be found that these sinners have a great many followers in many parts of the country. But we are told that these people were misled. How often have we not been told by the right hon. gentleman and his friends that on their side is found the cream of the representative intelligence of the various provinces in this Dominion. From the province of Quebec they have 54 out of 65 members, and they boast that these 65 comprise the best educated men from that province-men who know the people's

wants and are capable of educating the people. Yet the supporters of the right hon. gentleman went down to the county of Drummond-Arthabaska and put the policy of the government before the people and explained that policy to the people as best they could, and now they come back and tell us that the people were misled. What were the government and their friends' doing? They had plenty of money, and any number of missionaries, and yet they failed in their attempt to educate these people. Can it be that these people are so illiterate that they cannot be taught? That is practically in effect what the right hon. gentleman and his friends are now arguing when they say that the electors in Drummond-Arthabaska were deluded and misled into giving a verdict which they never would have given had they understood what they were doing. But what a slur is that on the followers of the right hon. gentleman who went down to that county and worked assiduously to convince the electors? There must be something radically wrong. We are told that there was any amount of whisky and everything else that could be desired to win the election, yet notwithstanding all that the verdict of the people went against the government. To my mind that verdict is rather complimentary to their intelligence. It shows that th'ey understood what influences were brought to bear on them and they deserve great credit for having resisted all these demoralizing influences and given such a plain and straight verdict on this most important question. The race cry, we are told, was raised down there against the government. Well, if that be the case, hon. gentlemen opposite were only beaten at their own game. I remember going to a show when I was a boy and seeing the three card monte men gathering in the money of the unsophiscated who tried their hand at the game. All the boys gathered around these men and started to play and of course lost their money. Then the three card montes became unpopular, and the sharpers started games at cards, and the boys again lost their money. Finally, there came along an old stager, who took a hand in the game and cleaned out the whole bunch. Then the sharpers who were cleaned out sent for the police to have the old man arrested. That exactly illustrates the tactics of the party opposite. They come back and squeal because they were beaten at their own game.
Why are the people of Canada to-day afraid of this question? If that same question was submitted to the rural constituencies in Ontario, I believe that seven-tenths of them would give practically the same verdict against it. Why? Because they have never been consulted and because they know it is the commencement of an expenditure which will be very oner-Mr. SPROTJLE
ous, they do not know where the policy will lead and it is being imposed on them without their being consulted. They know what we are spending for defence to-day. On militia and defence we spent in 1896 $1,136,000. What was it last year? $4,679,000, nearly $5,000,000. The capital expendi-diture for this purpose in 1896 was $1,000,000 and in 1910 $1,299,000. In other words the expenditure on militia and defence has grown from $2,000,000 in 1896 to nearly $6,000,000 in 1910, not counting the expenditure that must take place during the current year for this beautiful navy. The First Minister has told us that the navy will cost this year between $3,000,000 and $4,000,000, and this expenditure will rise to nearly $10,000,000 next year. Then it must inevitably and rapidly rise. Is it any wonder that the people of Canada are reluctant to be committed to such an undertaking without knowing what kind of a navy they will get or whether it will be useful? It is because of that and of the growing spirit of militiarism so apparent in Canada of late years, that the people are becoming alarmed and are distrustful of the government who are introducing this policy. Our naval expenditure next year may be $10,000,000. A few years hence it will be $20,000,000 then $25,000,000 and then $30,000,000, going up all the time, but yet the government supporters say the people are satisfied. The people have never been allowed to say whether they are satisfied or not. The present government dare not trust and consult the people because if they did they would get a verdict that would tell them to discontinue their present policy.
The Minister of Marine and the Navy said that there are three reasons why the government are compelled to carry out this policy, first to guard our coasts, second to guard our commerce against pirates and third to maintain the supremacy of the British Empire. Let any one examine this beautiful navy as proposed to the people of Canada and ask himself how7 far it will fulfil these purposes. We have a coast to protect ten times as long as the coast of the British Isles. How far would this navy be able to protect that coast if there was any danger of any marauders coming into our country to interfere -with our rights. One vessel at Esquimalt, another at Halifax that could not catch the greatest lubber of a pirate ship that ever travelled on the high seas! Yet it is to protect our coasts. In my judgment beyond these two points it is absolutely useless to protect our coasts and I think the Canadian people have long since reached the same conclusion. Could it guard our commerce? No, because it could not leave our ports, it w7as not intended to leave our ports. The Minister of Marine read us

blood-curdling stories about some piratical excursions that were carried on away down in Mexico, and near Shanghai and indicated that we wanted a navy to protect our commerce and catch these pirates. He spoke too of the ' Princess May ' which was taken away by one of these pirates and brought back by Chinese war vessels. We wanted this navy to go after them. What an exhibition it would be, the greatest laughing stock Canada ever saw or heard of. They say it is to protect our commerce on the high seas, but we were told the navy was not to leave our ports unless in company with the British navy, which would come and escort it out of our ports so that it might fight with them. It dare not go out alone because the vessels might be run down and taken for they could do nothing without an order in council authorizing them to shoot. The minister tells us that is why we must build a navy. I think the intelligent people will laugh at it, and at its ability to protect our coasts, owing to their length, nature and difficulty, it will be absolutely useless for that purpose. It will be of no use to protect our commerce on the high seas, it can never go out on the high seas. The minister recalled what we have done to protect the fisheries and to enforce the law and look after illegal fishermen. But it is not to go on the high seas.
Then we are told as the greatest and most important reason that it is to help to maintain the supremacy of the British Empire. If that was the reason why did the government not follow the suggestion of the British people, and build the ships as they ought to be built if they are to be used for that purpose. They refused to do it, and therefore I am inclined to be somewhat skeptical as to whether that was in the hon. gentleman's mind when he proposed it-I do not think it was. If it was for that purpose why do they not let it cooperate with the British navy in maintaining the supremacy of the British Empire? Why is it they will not allow it to go out until there is an order in council or parliament has given authority ? It does not look as if that was the intention, and then they go to the province of Quebec and assure the people that this navy is to protect our shores, it was never intended to go on the high seas. We are told it is to maintain the supremacy of the British Empire. That is a very praiseworthy aim, but the conduct of the minister, and of the First Minister, and the policy that they have evolved for that purpose give the lie to the whole thing because the navy could not possibly be useful for that purpose as it is organized to-day. For these reasons as well as for others, I shall support the amendment to the amendment proposed by the hon. the
leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) primarily because it aims at doing what the Conservative party have always been willing and desirous to do, appeal to the people for their verdict, before we commit ourselves and the country to such a great and important undertaking.

speechtext:
Of course, we all have to stand by what we say. I want to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, the attitude the opposition takes on this question and the attitude that is taken by the government. It is not very long ago, I do not need to go back and read what was said by the Prime Minister 16 years ago. This subject of the desirability of establishing a Canadian navy was first brought to the attention of this House by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), in what was considered to be a very admirable speech, and he closed it by moving this motion:-
That in the opinion of this House, in view of her great and varied resources, of her geographical position and national environ-

ments, and of that spirit of self-help and selfrespect which alone befits a strong and growing people, Canada should no longer delay in assuming her proper share of the responsibility and financial burden incident to the suitable protection of her exposed coast line and great sea ports.
I say that the speech with which he preceded that resolution was an able and argumentative one, but in it the hon. member failed to make it clear as to whether he himself was in favour of a direct contribution to the British Empire, or whether we should have a navy of our own, hut I think I may say he strongly leaned to the side that, as it was proposed in his resolution, our self-respect should lead us to establish a navy of our own. Of course, it was well known that the views of the Liberal party were not fully expressed in that resolution, and the Prime Minister moved an amendment thereto in the following words:-
This House fully recognizes the duty of the people of Canada as they increase in numbers and wealth, to assume in larger measure the responsibilities of national defence.
The House reaffirms the opinion, repeatedly expressed by representatives of Canada, that under the present constitutional relations between the mother country and the selfgoverning dominions, the payment of any stated contribution to the imperial treasury for naval and military purposes would not, so far as Canada is concerned, he a satisfactory solution of the question of defence.
The House has observed with muck satisfaction the relief afforded in recent years of the taxpayers of the United Kingdom through the assumption by the Canadian people of considerable military expenditure formerly charged upon the imperial treasury.
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested by the Admiralty at the last imperial conference, and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Great Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the empire and the peace of the world.
The House expresses its firm conviction that whenever the need arises the Canadian people will he found ready and willing to make any sacrifice that is required to give to the imperial authorities the most loyal and hearty co-operation in every movement for the maintenance of the integrity and the honour of the empire.
When he resumed his seat the leader of the opposition, commenting upon the resolution, expressed himself as favourable to it. He suggested some amendment, he suggested dropping one of the paragraphs, which was, I think, paragraph 3, which alluded to what we had done in the way of assuming the duty of looking after the defences of Esquimalt and Halifax; he thought it would be better if we omitted that. I Mr. PATERSON.
think my hon. friend stated that he wished nothing to stand in the way of an unanimous resolution being adopted by this House, which was earnestly desired by himself, by the hon. member for North Toronto, and he trusted by every member in the House. Then he suggested another amendment, and that was the insertion of only one word in what was then section 4 of the Prime Minister's resolution. These two suggestions of -the leader of the opposition were assented to by the right hon. the leader of the government. So we amended his resolution in that direction, and as thus amended the resolution carried.

I will read clause 2 as finally passed. I read to the House the resolution as it was proposed, and I have stated the emendations that were offered by the leader of the opposition, and what he suggested was agreed to by the Prime Minister, the resolution was amended in the direction that he asked for by the insertion of a- word in paragraph 4. This was done by the Prime Minister at the suggestion of the leader of the opposition, and unanimously accepted by the House. I have alluded to what was dropped, I have said he wanted an addition of one word in paragraph 4. I will read paragraph 4:-
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested by the Admiralty at the last imperial conference, and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Great Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the empire and the peace of the world.
Well, Sir, what was that word that the leader of the opposition wanted to have added to that section, that section which expressed the approval of this House in the creation of a naval service? What was that word? Well, it was this-if he likes, I will read it from the ' Hansard ' as it is found on page 3521:-
Just one word as to a further amendment which I would like to suggest to my right hon. friend. In paragraph 4, he proceeds:
The House will cordially approve of any necessary expenditure designed to promote the organization of a Canadian naval service in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested

by the Admiralty at the last imperial conference, and in full sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Great Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the empire and the peace of the world.
I would be glad if my right lion, friend could accept the suggestion of inserting in that paragraph some word which would indicate an intention to act promptly. If my right hon. friend would insert before the word ' organization ' some such word as ' immediate ' or even ' early,' I think it would greatly improve the paragraph, it wrould meet with my approval, and I do not think it would be disapproved of by any hon. member of this House.
The Prime Minister accepted it and he put in the word ' speedy.' While there was the declaration on the part of the Prime Minister in his resolution that wg should do this, it was not enough for the leader of the opposition. He said, I want this thing to be done at once. 1 want the word ' immediate ' in; and now the whole cry of the opposition who voted for it is: Do not go into this until you ask the people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker; when the House rose at six o'clock I had pointed out from the records what had occurred in the session of 1909 with reference to the Canadian navy. I showed from the records of parliament that this House had then unanimously agreed upon the construction of a Canadian navy. I pointed out that the Prime Minister in his resolution which was accepted unanimously by the House, had not fixed a definite time for the commencement of that work, and that point being noted by the leader of the opposition the suggestion was adopted that the House should declare for the early construction of a Canadian navy, and, on the suggestion of the leader of the opposition the Prime Minister, consented that the word ' speedy ' should be added. The unanimous resolution of the House was that the government should not take any more time than was absolutely necessary to consider this question, and that they should proceed with the navy immediately. What hon. gentlemen opposite, and what this House unanimously voted for was the speedy construction of a Canadian navy. Well, the government of the day, and the Minister of Marine, in accordance with the expressed desire of the House (hon. gentlemen opposite included) desired that there should be speed in reference to this matter, and after consultation with the naval authorities in Britain, within less than a year they brought down a measure to this House,
and so met the view of the 'speedy ' party as I may call the gentlemen opposite. Unfortunately for me when the Bill of the Minister of Marine was laid before the House empowering him to go on with the work that a year before was considered so urgent, I was in a distant part of the empire, where telegraphic rates are heavy and where but very condensed items of Canadian news appeared in the newspapers. But, one fine morning I learned that the second reading of the Navy Bill had been opposed by the leader of the opposition and this item in the West Indian papers purported to set forth that the leader of the opposition had suggested that the Bill should be hung up until there had been an expression of the will of the people on it and their approval obtained. But, meanwhile without consulting the people himself, the leader of the opposition proposed that we were to take $25,000,000 of the money of the people of Canada and hand it over to the British authorities to be spent where and how they might choose. I thought there must be surely something wrong in that because a short year before the leader of the opposition and his followers were anxious for the speedy construction of this navy, and I did not see how in the year 1910 they desired to consult the people before any speed was exhibited. I could not believe my eyes when I saw it stated that the leader of the opposition wanted to consult the people with reference to the construction of a Canadian navy of which the House, mark you, had approved the previous session, when, at that same session he was ready to hand over $25,000,000 at once without the consent of the people. We are told by gentlemen opposite that they did not vote for a plebiscite last session, and in fact that they were opposed to it ; but I quote this paragraph from their amendment :
That no permanent policy should be entered upon involving large future expenditures of this character until it has been submitted to the people and has received their approval.
For my part I do not know how it otherwise could receive or not receive the approval of the people, and at that stage, except by way of plebiscite. Talk about devious ways and diverse views, but I do not think you will find in the history of any legislative assembly a political party occupying such a peculiar position on any public question as gentlemen opposite occupy to-day on this naval question. There is a change in the amendment offered this year when compared with their amendment of last year. They then made the excuse that the terms of the Bill did not just suit them, and if that be so they should have moved amendments to

those sections of the Bill of which they did not approve.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: tR (Leeds). So they did.

speechtext:
They did. Yes; but that does not affect the question of consulting the people. The people were to be consulted on the principle of whether we were to have a Canadian navy, and not on the details of the Bill.
I come now to consider another change on the part of hon. members" opposite. The amendments proposed to this address are as follows: The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) moves in amendment:
That the said motion he amended by adding to the proposed Address to His Excellency the Governor General the following paragraph at the end thereof:-
The House regrets that the speech from the Throne gives no indication whatever of the intention of the government to consult the people on its naval policy and the general question of the contribution of Canada to imperial armaments.
And the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) is not quite satisfied with the verbiage of that amendment, and moves the following:
That all the words after the word ' thereof ' in the proposed motion in amendment be omitted and the following substituted therefor:-
We beg to assure Your Excellency of the unalterable attachment and devotion of the people of Canada to the British Crown and of their desire and intention to fulfil all just responsibilities devolving upon this country as one of the nations of the empire. We desire, however, to express our regret that Your Excellency's gracious speech gives no indication whatever of any intention on the part of Your Excellency's advisers to consult the people on the naval policy of Canada,
The House will observe that the proposal to kill off the project of building a Canadian navy is embraced in this as well as in the amendment of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. It seems to me that hon. members opposite are not in as good a position as they were in last year. Why? Because, if no preparation for defence is to be made until a general election, two years hence, what position do they occupy? Last year, recognizing that something ought to be done and done promptly, these hon. gentlemen suggested the alternative of giving $25,000,000 to the British government as a contribution towards imperial defence. This, they said, would provide for two Dreadnoughts, and these could be earmarked, so that, in case of danger arising for Canada, we could ask that they be sent to defend our coasts. But there is nothing in this amendment to suggest that we are to do anything in the matter of Canadian self-defence until the people have Mr. PATERSON.
been consulted. We are to stop building our own navy until after another general election, and meanwhile we are to do nothing. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) sits there and smiles. He may well smile. Why does not the leader of the opposition propose this year, as he proposed last year, that, stopping the construction of a Canadian navy, we ought to give a grant to the British Empire? Is it because the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, whom they tried to read out of their party, not only remains in their party, but has assumed the leadership of it?

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: You are not serious, surely?

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
I am serious. Might it be-of course we are merely looking around, making suppositions and trying to understand this matter-might it be that the whip of the party, feeling nervous because of a telegram that he had sent that would identify his party, or, at least identify himself with the Nationalist party, thought : Well, now, I am not going to be singled out in this matter; I am going to see to it that the leader of the opposition shall take the same position that I have taken; he has got to move a resolution that will suit the hon. member for Jacques Cartier; he has got to do the very thing that will convince the people of Canada that there is an understanding between the Nationalist and Conservative parties? Can it be that the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. George Taylor) and the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) are nervous over this matter and sought to get the leader of their party thus committed because he was smiling to find that, while he was denounced personally by the Nationalists, and tried to keep clear of the strife being out of the country during part of the time this strife was on-as I believe was the case-these hon. gentlemen had bound and committed themselves by what they had said and written in regard to the Nationalist party? Did these hon. gentlemen cause their leader to virtually accept the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, and, in order to please him, tie their party up with the Nationalists by proposing to this House to stop all arrangements for building a Canadian navy for two years, and prevent any single step in the direction of naval defence, either by building a navy or by contribution to the navy of Great Britain? What position are these hon. members in who themselves had suggested speedy action in this matter on the part of the government? The government's course was clear and unmistakable. They had received the mandate of the House, and that mandate was not coupled with any suggestion, even the remotest, that the matter should be referred to the people.

The resolution of the House called for speedy action, and the Minister of Marine acted speedily. When hon. members opposite moved last year that the building of a Canadian navy should not proceed, at least they had the patriotism and decency to propose to do something. If they were to stop the building of a navy under the minister, at least they proposed a contribution to the British government which might be used in such a way as to secure the defence of our own coasts. But there is no such provision or suggestion now. This resolution baldly says: Stop all work on the Canadian navy until you have the approval of the Canadian people. And at the same time, they tell us they do not believe in a plebiscite. That means to wait for a general election, and, meanwhile, do nothing. Ah, what will their imperialist friends in the old country think of this? What will their imperialist friends in this country think of this?

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext:
Yes, I wonder what they will think of it when they realize that this patriotic opposition are neither for building a Canadian navy nor for a contribution to the British government to grant us aid in protecting our coasts. I can understand my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor), a man after my own heart-ready to fight; when he makes a speech is willing to stay in the House and listen to the reply; I admire him for that. Therefore, as he is leading the opposition to-night-I beg my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule's) pardon; he is in his place. He is a fighter and I admire him for that. I suppose my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule), when he meets with some of his Conservative friends and they ask him this question:	'You voted less than two
years ago for a speedy construction of a navy, but this session you voted to stop that, how do you account for the change?- I suppose my hon. friend will try and fasten the blame on the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur). When his supporters say to him: A year ago you voted to give $25,000,000 to Great Britain to build some war ships-that was something doing -but this year you have dropped that, have you been swung round by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier?-When this question is put to him by loyal patriotic members of the Conservative party, I suppose he will say to them-My dear friends it is true-we did not mention in our resolution of this year anything about sending $25,000,000 to build Dreadnoughts, but you must remember this. You must remember that we did beg to assure His Excellency Lord Grey of the unalterable attachment and devotion of the people of Canada to the empire. But it seems to me that the hon. gentleman would 12
be very apt to meet this reply from his patriotic friends-You have issued so much of that paper currency out of the bank of Tory loyalty and that the people have begun to find out that there is no gold basis of action behind it, and that currency has become so utterly depreciated that no responsible ship-builder would take a carload of it for a fishing smack. What else could they say:	Oh,
but my hon. friend would reply, we not only professed unalterable attachment to the British Crown, but also our desire and intention to fulfil all just responsibility devolving upon this country as one of the dominions of the empire. Well, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), who seems to think that Canada has already fully discharged all her duties and responsibilities to the British Crown, could vote for that expression of sentiment. I have never heard him say that he was not prepared to do what he considered the just responsibilities devolving upon him. It is for every man's conscience to determine for himself what he ought to do. What may be considered the just by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, the just responsibilities that devolve upon us, I cannot say because I cannot read his mind. Rather less than a year ago he said we should hand over $25,000,000 to Great Britain, but he has now dropped that policy and taken up the same line as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, who thinks that we are doing quite well enough in building railways and looking after our fortifications.
But what are we to do? Are we to leave the country wholly without defence? Is no step to be taken by us to defend ourselves or give aid to Great Britain? That is the stand taken by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. He would put a stop to the efforts of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, although less than two years ago he voted for the speedy construction of a navy. My hon. friend certainly would make a remarkable success as a lightning change artist.
An hon. gentleman opposite has made the suggestion that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, feeling that he was losing the province of Quebec, was trying to appeal to the imperialistic sympathies of the other provinces.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says hear, hear. Will he point out to me where there was an appeal made by the Prime Minister which was not made to the loyal and patriotic men of all the provinces? But I can well understand that many men in the Conservative party, utterly disgusted with the procedure of the opposition in attempting to obstruct the building of a Canadian navy and yet not sending a dollar to Britain, will throw off their party allegiance



and refuse longer to support men who are standing on the very ground the Nationalists stand upon. No Canadian built navy, no aid to Great Britain, no defence of this country-such a policy, it would be natural to suppose, would alienate those men who had hitherto supported the leader of the opposition. They would say to themselves: While we may not have seen eye to eye with the Prime Minister on many an occasion, we do see that in obedience to the command of the House of Commons-for it was a command-to go on and take steps for the defence of this empire, he is carrying out that command, even though it may lose him for the time being support in the province of Quebec, and that is one reason why all men who believe in what is just, right, patriotic and straightforward should stand behind him. My right hon. friend makes no appeal to any particular section, but to honest men of every province. What the result may be, I do not know, I make no prophecy at all. I only_suggest what seems to me would be very reasonable conduct on the part of men who believe that a government should be straightforward and consistent and that they should support a party who feel bound by the responsibilities of office to take some step in order that protection may be afforded this country, now consisting of eight millions of people, in order that our own coast be protected, and that we may come to the relief of the mother country, when that relief is needed, and' not leave on her the whole burden.
If you were ready a year ago to vote your $25,000,000 because there was danger and our navy could not be ready in time to render effective aid, if there was danger of a war then, why is the danger not greater this year, when you are dropping your $25,000,000? Every year that passes brings that war nearer and nearer, if it is to come. Then, why drop your $25,000,000? Why refuse to give it on the ground that Canada must consult the people before entering on a naval scheme? Why not add to your resolution what you did last year, that meanwhile the safety of the empire and the honour of Canada demand that we should place two Dreadnoughts or their price in the hands of the British admiralty? Why not? Is it in deference to the tender feelings of the now-shall I say?-almost apparent to many people, leader of the combined Tory and Nationalist party?

speechtext:
I acquiesce at once in the references that have been made by hon. gentlemen to the large and increasing trade of Canada and the universal prosperity of the Canadian people. In looking over the address of His Excellency I notice one very serious omission which I would call to the attention of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). Reference is made to the death of our late Mr. PATERSON.
King, Edward VII., but no mention whatever is made of the accession to the Throne of King George the Fifth. Surely the right hon. gentleman has overlooked this event, so important to the British Empire and to the people of Canada.
The people of Ontario, the people of Canada will be very much disappointed when they read the speech of the hon. the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson). If ever there was an important question in which the people of Canada are interested, it is this naval policy of the government. When other important public questions have been dealt with in this parliament they have been communicated through the press to the people of Canada, but until within a very short time the people of Canada were altogether out of touch on the naval proposition and do not understand this great and important question. The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) tried to make some small political capital, as he generally does in the House, from that important word inserted in the resolution of tyro years ago by the leader of the opposition ' speedy.' I think he said he would style the Liberal-Conservative party the speedy party of Canada. I do not think the people of Canada would so style the present administration. The right hon. gentleman and the Minister of Customs, when in opposition, made some very important promises to the people of Canada, but they have not been very speedy in fulfilling those promises. I remember the Minister of Customs making promises to the people of Ontario. One of his promises was that when their party came into power they would abolish protection. There has been no speedy fulfilment of that promise. He also said they would abolish the Senate. There has been no speedy fulfilment of that promise either. I could enumerate many other promises by that hon. gentleman, .and therefore I say there is no danger of this government being styled speedy from their manner of fulfilling the promises which they gave to the people.
The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) was very anxious to know what the Liberal-Conservative party would do in respect to the lands in the west of Canada. One of the planks laid down by the hon. the leader of the opposition in the well known Halifax platform of August 20, 1907, reads:-
The restoration of the public lands to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan upon fair terms.
Surely the hon. gentleman was not serious when hie asked what the leader of the Conservative party and the leader of the opposition meant by that; it is a plain statement of fact. Behind that there is a history [DOT] of the two parties in respect of the lands of the west. When the question of the auto-

nomy of the two western provinces wras under discussion the important question to which I have referred was discussed in the House. The Liberal-Conservative party, by its leader and other prominent men on this side of the House, stated clearly and distinctly to the people of Canada their policy in respect to the lands and minerals of those two provinces. I would, however, refer my hon. friend and the members from the west to the resolution to be found in the ' Votes and Proceedings ' of 1905, at page 823. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) moved a resolution that all lands, minerals and mines within the limits of the provinces shall belong to the provinces. At the very first opportunity, when the Liberal-Conservative party had to put themselves on record, when these provinces were being formed, when the Bills were before the House for discussion, before the final act had taken place in this parliament, the Liberal-Conservative party put themselves on record and said that in their opinion the lands and the minerals of these two western provinces should belong to the people and be vested in the local legislatures.
For that resolution the Liberal Conservative party in this House voted, but it was voted down by this_ government, and if there is any complaint from the west, as we know there is, because the lands and minerals are not vested in the legislatures of those provinces, the fault does not lie on this side of the House, but it lies with the right hon. gentleman and the Minister of Customs, and the friends of my hon. friend who is making a complaint in the House to-night. I have in my hand a despatch sent to the Toronto 1 News * two or three days ago, where a Liberal member of the Alberta legislature moved a resolution asking the legislature to declare that the lands, minerals and mines should be vested in the legislature of that province. That was not a. complaint from a Liberal-Conservative, that was a resolution moved by a prominent Liberal within the last ten days, directing the attention of the people of Canada to the gross negligence of this government in refusing to entrust the people of that province, as the people of the province of Ontario are entrusted, with the management of their lands and minerals in the interest of the people.
Is it of any advantage, Mr. Speaker, for the provincial government to own those lands and minerals? I think it is. In the province of Ontario, you understand, these lands, minerals and mines are vested in the local government. I have here a statement of the revenue derived by the treasury of the province from those resources; the statement covers ten months ending the 31st of October, 1909. I give the figures for ten months, because the fiscal year of 12$
that government was changed, like the fiscal year of this government, so that I take the latest figures available. For the ten months ending 31st October, 1909, the lands, forests and mines of that province yielded a revenue of $2,028,224.48. During those ten months the province of Ontario expended for agricultural purposes-and I would direct the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture to this fact; he will not be surprised, I am sure, because he has heard it before, but it will be a surprise to the people of Canada to know that the provin?e of Ontario expends more eveiy year on agriculture in that province than the Dominion of Canada does in the management of our agricultural resources by the Minister of Agriculture. The Ontario government expended on agriculture in those ten months, $493,410.19; and on education, $1,452,162.11, or a total on agriculture and education of $1,945,572.30. The province received during those ten months from their minerals, mines and forests, $82,652.18 more than was expended on both agriculture and education. Therefore it is of some importance to the people of western Canada that they should own their mines, their minerals and their timber wealth; it would be a great advantage to them. When I hear hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House talking about the centralization of power, I am reminded that the Liberal party and the Liberal government refused by voice, by speech and by vote to give to the people of western Canada their rights when they -were passing the Autonomy Bills in 1905.
The hon. the Minister of Customs was very anxious to get a statement of the policy of the Liberal-Conservative party on the naval question. He was more anxious to obtain a statement of our policy than he was to point the people of Canada to the policy of his own government. If you noticed it, he said very little about the policy of his own party and his own government; but he seemed to be-should I say that he did not understand our policy? I must not say that, because he is an experienced politician and a member of this government. The hon. gentleman, of course, did not expect that we on this side of the House would take him seriously. We have heard the hon. gentleman talking partisanship before in this House, and we understand it very well. It was not so bad coming from a gentleman occupying, as he did, for so long, a humble seat on the opposition side of the House, when he was going up and down this country telling the people what they ought to have. The people of this country were not so much interested then as they are now in the remarks of the hon. gentleman. But while he occupies an important position in the government, he does not seem to have lost
351)

that habit of making stump speeches, and he will persist in inflicting them on the House, whether he is in the government or out of it. Whether the hon. gentleman does or does not understand the policy of the Liberal-Conservative party on the naval question, is not very important just now; the people of Canada seem to understand the government policy and the people of Drummond-Arthabaska seem to have a little knowledge of it as well. Whatever was said in that election campaign, either on one side or the other, is not a question for ine to discuss here; that is a matter I presume which will be dealt with by the electors of that county. I do not know what was said. But whatever may be said of the speeches that were made in Drummond-Arthabaska, there is one thing clear, and that is that the electors of that county, a county that had formerly elected Liberal members for many years, have declared at the polls that they are opposed to the policy_ of this government on the naval question, and they 'have consequently sent a gentleman to this House in opposition to the government on that question, though he calls himself a Liberal on other questions. That is the latest voice from the Canadian people, and it seems to have had some effect upon this government, it has worried them a lot. They were suggesting that they might open some other seats; I do not think there is much likelihood of the Senate being reformed by this government opening any other Quebec seats for the next three or four months.
During the recess I discussed this naval proposition before the electors of the county which I have the honour to represent. I put the matter fairly before them, not in a partisan way, but from a higher standpoint, because I knew that the electors of the county of Peel were anxious ro understand the respective attitudes of the two parties upon this great question. I stated clearly and distinctly that because we believed that an emergency existea in the old country, the Liberal-Conservative party put forward a resolution in view of that emergency, and we stated that if such emergency existed the Liberal-Conservative party were willing to vote a sum of money to be sent to Great Britain to help her in her hour of need. There is no misunderstanding about our policy in that regard. The Liberal-Conservative party in this House spoke in favour of it, voted in favour of it, and the Liberal-Conservative party throughout Canada understand it quite well. Why then, should the Minister of Customs struggle with that question in the House for fifteen minutes? True, he makes the statement that he was absent from the country. Well, he left some person behind but when I was listening to him discuss this matter I thought he had been absen' Mr. BLAIN.
from the House. Surely, if the hon. gentleman had been in his place and heard the discussion he would never have ventured to struggle with the resolutions moved by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. Surely he would have understood them well. The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) understood the policies of the three parties. My . hon. friend nods his assent to that. Therefore, he differs from the Minister of Customs in the government of which he was a supporter. The hon. member for Beauce pointed out the difference between the policies in the three parties, if you may call them three parties.

speechtext:
politics. Let me ask the Minister of Customs, whether in the passage of that resolution of 1909 the Liberal-Conservative party did pot show its willingness to take the question out of partisan discussion? Did we not join hands with the government and say: We are prepared to assist you if you will carry out the suggestions coming from the old land, from the people who understand the naval defence of the empire better than the Prime Minister of Canada or the Minister of Customs; if you will carry out the policy suggested by the British Admiralty and the British government so that when our navy is constructed it shall be one with the British navy, then the Liberal-Conservative party of Canada will be one with the Liberal government if the electors in a general election express in favour of such a policy. But, having departed altogether from the proposition of the British Admiralty on this question it ill-becomes them to charge the Liberal-Conservative party with bad faith. I hurl the insinuation back at the Minister of Customs and I tell him that in respect to the noncarrying out of that resolution the sinners are on his side of the House and not on this side. The Liberal-Conservative party have always been willing to consult and trust the people of Canada as is clearly demonstrated by the history of our party. The project of building the Canadian Pacific railway was of great interest to the people of this country; that railway was to carry the surplus population from the east to the west and to bring the products of the great west to the east and thence to the old land; it involved the expenditure of millions of dollars and millions of acres of land owned by the people of Canada, and Sir John Macdonald, leader of the Conservative party then in power did not venture to tie up the people of this country with that project without consulting them and obtaining their mandate. In 1878 when the industries of Canada languished; when the Liberal party which now boasts of its loyalty to Canada and Great Britain was in power and when their Finance Minister told the people that the government were but as flies upon the wheel to help them, the right hon. Sir John Macdonald, then in opposition, said to the people of Canada we are prepared to take this issue before you and on it we will stand or fall; we are willing to trust the people.
