speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to offer one or two observations affecting certain aspects of this debate. I was impressed by the attitude and the spirit of jubilation shown by gentlemen on the opposition side of the House when they met here to discharge their duties as representatives of this country. The hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) made the statement that in his opinion the government were in mortal dread of a general election, that the First Minister had lost his prestige in the province of Quebec, that his prestige and his influence had been shattered. I naturally made some inquiry to see what had happened during the year to arouse the hitherto drooping spirits of the opposition and to make them feel that, after having wandered so many years in the wilderness of opposition, they saw in the future, somewhat distant still, a time when they would be recalled to discharge the duties of government.
In looking over the files of the Ottawa
' Citizen ' I observe an item in that paper bearing date November 13, 1909 :
For two hours yesterday Conservative senators and members took counsel in caucus upon matters affecting the party's political welfare. At some length the question was discussed of the time and place for holding the great Conservative convention of 1910. The leader's proposal met with enthusiastic support, but arrangement of details was deferred for the time being.
In the Ottawa ' Citizen ' of November 27, I find :
A sub-committee of the Conservative caucus has been appointed to consider the time and place of the general convention of the party next year. It will be held some time during the summer, and the idea of holding it during the session does not meet with much favour. Ottawa, Toronto and Winnipeg each has it advocates.
So that at that date they were 'still considering the advisability of having a party convention. Under date of December 1, I find this item :
While a sub-committee of the Conservative caucus which is considering the time And place of holding the general party convention has not yet reported and no decision has been reached, the impression seems to be growing that Ottawa will be selected. A number of western men who first favoured Winnipeg now think that from a strategical viewpoint it will be better to have the gathering at the capital, which being nearer the centre of the country, would ensure a representative attendance.
Under date December 8, I find :
Recommendations of sub-committee :-
(1)	That a committee of fifty, of whom not more than twenty should be M.Ps., to be known as a committee on preliminary arrangement for the Dominion Convention of the Liberal-Conservative party, be appointed by Mr. R. L. Borden.
(2)	That said committee be called together at Ottawa for their first meeting on some day in January, 1910.
(3)	That in the opinion of the sub-committee the Dominion convention should be held in the city of Winnipeg during the exhibition in September.
Subsequently there was a meeting of the committee on preliminary arrangements for the convention in Ottawa on January 24. The Ottaw.a ' Citizen ' of January 25, contained this statement:
The big convention of the Conservative party will be held in Ottawa, commencing on June 15 and 16 next. This was decided at the meeting of the general committee on arrangements representing all parts of the Dominion.
From this I learned that it was the intention of the Conservative party to call a convention of their supporters from all parts of the Dominion for the purpose of

formulating a common policy upon which all should stand and fight the battle in the coming election. It was stated that the great convention held by the Liberal party in 1893 at which they formulated a policy upon which they stood and appealed to the people, had been a great factor in winning the battle for the Liberal party and it was felt that it would not be bad policy to follow that successful example. But the convention was not held and I wondered if it was that fact that accounted for the spirit of jubilation to be observed in the speech of the member for Yale-Cariboo. Perhaps he felt that the holding of a convention would be rather a serious matter for the great Conservative party. He may have felt that under the circumstances it might be difficult to get the different wings of the Conservative party to stand on a common platform. The crisis was passed by the very simple alternative of having no convention at all and the hon. gentlemen may have felt that the Conservative party had something to be thankful for, even if they did not win an election during 1910. The jubilation of the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo and other hon. gentlemen on his side of the House may be partly accounted for by what occurred at a meeting held in the town of Trenton, Ontario, in June, 1910. At that meeting there were present the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), and Hon. Sir Mackenzie Bowell, who was at one time leader of the Conservative party. Sir Mackenzie Bowell there delivered a speech irom which I shall read a quotation :
He congratulated Mr. Borden on the selection of ex-Judge Doherty as his lieutenant. He is m every sense worthy of the position. He is an honest man, whose public and private actions are prompted by the highest ideals. He is one of the same class of men as Sir John Thompson. He will be loyal to his leader, and loyal to his principles. He abhors trickery and duplicity. The Conservative party gains by his association with Mr. Borden, a leader of whom it is proud/
At the same meeting there was a speech delivered by Mr. J. W. Johnson, member of the Ontario Legislature for the county of West Hastings. Mr. Johnson made the following statement:-
When Mr. Borden is called upon to form a cabinet we shall require from him that it shall contain no man whose record is tainted, no matter how eminent his services to the party may have been in the past. The Conservative party cannot afford to carry any man who has used time or money to his own advantage that he owed to the business in which he was employed, or from the management of a company to promote his own interests. The Conservative party has carried that burden too long.

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the Conservative party have got rid of that burden, I presume it did have some effect in rousing the spirits and enthusiasm of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. The reorganization which was announced some months ago took place to the extent intimated by Mr. Johnson in his speech at Trenton. They felt that after having suffered from the handicap I have mentioned for so many years when they were now relieved they would be in a better position to win the electorate of this Dominion on the great question of public policy. I am not going to make any observations as to the advantages that are likely to accrue to the Conservative party by reason of this reorganization and by reason of their having got rid of the burden which they carried so long. But I venture to say that if the reorganization is carried to the extent this gentleman refers to, then the criticisms directed by hon. gentlemen on the opposition side as respects the policy of the government will be very much less interesting and entertaining if that hon. gentleman is not in his place as he has been heretofore.
The hon. member also referred to a tour which was made by the First Minister throughout the west during last summer. I think it will be conceded that from every point of view that tour was a great success. I think it will be conceded by hon. gentlemen who sit on the opposition side that the people of the west were glad to avail themselves of the opportunity of coming forward to hear what the first man in Canada had to say on great public questions, and what were the plans and what were the policies he had in view for the future. But there were other political tours in Canada, to one of which I will refer, that took place in the province of Nova Scotia. The hon. the leader of the opposition, in the month of August, decided to address some public meetings in the province of Nova Scotia. The Halifax ' Herald ' of August 11, referring to the first meeting of the tour, which took place at Truro, has this to say:-
The fact that so large a crewd gathered to hear Mr. Borden is noteworthy in view of the fact that Howe's circus billed for a week before was showing in the town at the same hour.
Now, there is no intimation in that despatch of any enormous crowd of people coming forward to hear what the leader of the opposition had to say on the naval question, for instance, or on any other great question of policy. The fact is all the more striking when we remember that he had as his assistant on that occasion the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers), whose well known forensic and histrionic talents did not even avail to draw the crowd away from the attractions that were offered by the lady contortionist and by the pink

lemonade man. From Truro the leader of the -opposition went into the county of Guys-borough, and addressed a meeting there. The Halifax ' Herald ' of August 16, referring to the Guysborough meeting, says this:-
There was a packed meeting in the court house this afternoon, in spite of a typical hay day to hear Mr. R. L. Borden.
The leader of the opposition did not seem to have the same idea as regards the success of that meeting that the correspondent of the Halifax ' Herald ' did, because, in his interview which he gave in the city of Ottawa upon his return, he stated that his meetings were very successful with the exception of one in the town of Guys-borough, where the crowd was not large because it was a typical hay day, and the people attended to their work. The same is true with the other meetings that were held throughout the province of Nova Scotia ; one reason or another was alleged to account for the small attendance that went out to hear the leader of the opposition.	I am not
satisfied myself as to the value of these explanations, because a gentleman occupying the high position of leader of a great political party ought to be able to bring out the people in large numbers when he undertakes to instruct them upon any public question. I well remember another occasion when a leader of an opposition visited the province of Nova Scotia, and came to the town in which I live. On that occasion the circumstances were similar, it was in the hay making season, the weather was ideal for farm work, but nevertheless the people came out not only in hundreds but in thousands to hear what this gentleman had to say upon the questions in which they were interested. The tour on that occasion was made by the hon. gentleman who leads the government, but who at that time was leader of the opposition in this House. The people came forth in large numbers for the purpose of hearing him, although he did not have the prestige that he afterwards acquired from being the leader of a government. There was another tour projected by the leader of the opposition during the past summer, but which did not take place. A press despatch dated September 7 contained the following announcement:-

speechtext:
Borden is leaving for Toronto to confer with the various Conservative interests regarding his September tour in Ontario. There is every probability of the few present dates being cancelled, owing to the fact that the dates of the fall fairs are likely to he a serious hindrance to the success of any meetings.
At all events, we have no evidence at any of the receptions that were given to the
right hon. the first Minister on his tour in the west, of any enormous anxiety on the part of the people of Canada to put a sudden termination to his services as Prime Minister; there is no evidence available in any elections that were held during the last year to satisfy any inquiring mind that the government was losing the support, the sympathy or the confidence of the people which it has enjoyed to such a remarkable degree for so many years.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier, (Mr. Monk), in the speech which he delivered in this debate, made reference to- the fact that during the present year a constituency was lost to the government in the province of Quebec. That by-election has been so fully discussed and so thoroughly threshed out that I am not going to say anything about it, except to remark on the way the result of that election has roused the hopes and spirits of the opposition, although leading gentlemen belonging to the opposition have absolutely repudiated any part or interest in or connection with that election. Therefore, we cannot find in respect of that by-election the source of jubilation which has been indulged in by hon. gentlemen who have spoken on the other side of the House.
I would like, however, to make one or two observations by way of reply to the criticisms made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) in respect of that by-election. He referred to the fact that previous to 1896 there was a by-election held in the province of Quebec, and that although the Conservative party, then in power, had been able to hold its sway pretty thoroughly throughout that great province, on this particular occasion the government lost the by-election and the loss of that election sounded the death knell of the Conservative party as the governing body of this country. By-elections may be significant, or they may not be significant according to the circumstances and conditions under which they are run. If, in Drummond and Arthabaska, there was a vacancy sought to be filled by the candidates respectively of the two great parties of this Dominion-a Liberal candidate and a Conservative candidate-if the complete policy and record of the government had been placed before the people in that constituency, if they had been adjudged in the light of the manner in which these policies had been received and the Conservative party had won that election, I am quite willing to concede that the loss of a seat under these circumstances might have some significance as indicating that the government were losing some of the support that they had heretofore enjoyed. But, with respect to the by-election held in 1895, which was lost to the Conservative government, I very respectfully submit to the hon. mem-

ber for Jacques Cartier, and to other hon. gentlemen who are within sound of my voice, that other things happened between the losing of the by-election in the province of Quebec and the defeat of the Conservative government on the 23rd June, 1896.
It is not my desire to refer to matters that are unpleasant and disagreeable, but under all the circumstances I shall take the privilege of reminding you that between the time that the Conservative government lost that by-election in 1895 in the province of Quebec and the general election of 1896, there was an incident that took place in the history of the Conservative party that no hon. gentleman on this side desires wantonly to recall. There was an incident at which the whole people of the country stood aghast when one morning it was announced by the press of the country that six members of the government had proven false to their leader, had gone out of the cabinet and had taken a position which justified their leader in referring to them for all time afterwards as a nest of traitors. While the Liberal party will continue to perform their duties with proper regard to the interests of the country and the needs of the times, I think that the' right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) need not feel alarmed, or need not feel any chagrin over any by-election that will be lost to him under circumstances such as those which caused the loss of the seat in Drummond and Arthabaska.
This government has been performing a great work in the interests of this country, and it still has a very great work to perform. When we consider the enormous advances that have been made under the regime of this government with respect to the trade of the country, with respect to the facilities that have been given to the people in the way of railway and water transportation and other species of public advancement, and of public works, when we consider the record of the government as regards the revenues that have been brought in and the expenditures that have been made, when we consider what the government has done in increasing the trade and prosperity of the country, I think that the right hon. the leader of the government and the members who surround him in his cabinet need not be very much alarmed if once in a while an election is lost to them under the circumstances under which they lost the last one. While there is no advantage accruing to the Conservative party in respect of contests before the electorate, while the opposition to this government are making no further headway than they have made in the last twelve months with the people of Canada, I think we may rest assured that the government are still enjoying the confidence of the electorate quite as much as they have in the past.	*

maintopic: ADDRESS IN ANSWER TO HIS EXCELLENCY'S SPEECH.
speechtext:
On the question of reciprocity I desire to make one or two observations, although I realize that the hour is late and much has already been said on this question. I feel very strongly upon this question and I 4 do not agree with hon. gentlemen opposite, and the newspaper press supporting their party, in the assertion that the name of reciprocity should not be mentioned, but that it should be anathematized before the people of this country. I well remember during the session of parliament before the last, when prominent members of the opposition taunted and twitted members of the government because they had not kept their pledges to the people, and one of the pledges they alleged they had not kept was the pledge given in 1893 to bring about a reciprocity treaty with the United States. I do not know whether the circumstances and necessities are such as existed at that time, but I would myself hail with every satisfaction any measure of tariff reform or tariff reduction by this government that would further reduce the burdens of the people and solve, in so far as they are able to solve, the great question of the cost of living, which has aroused the people of the United States to an enormous degree within recent times.
There is much to be done by the government of this country with respect to all public matters, and I feel confident and assured that hon. gentlemen opposite will have small consolation coming to them with respect to the action of the electorate in the support which they will give to the government in the future.
Mr. LENNOX moved the adjournment of the debate..

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Fisher, House adjourned at 10.05 p.m.
Tuesday, November 29, 1910.
